speechtext: Why dines the Canadian sugar beet producer not receive a price equal to that paid on purchases made by the government sugar agency to cane growers in British West Indies, Cuba, Fiji and Santo Domingo?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The British Ministry of Food acts as agent for the Canadian sugar administration in purchases of cane sugar from abroad. These purchases are made from time to time, in consultation with the Canadian 5849-149J
authority, whenever, in the judgment of the buyer, prices are considered to be favourable. While the laid down cost of supplies for delivery in 1948 cannot yet be determined, depending as it does upon such variable factors as shipping costs, the average may exceed the existing ceiling price by a small amount. Since these purchases were made, however, the price of sugar on world markets has declined so that the Canadian ceiling does not depress domestic prices below the prices at which cane sugar could be laid down in Canada at the present time.

speechtext: -FILMS FOR EDUCATIONAL PURPOSES
What films, or film strips, have been released for educational work and for child and maternal health in the Department of National Health and Welfare?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The following health
education films and filmstrips, having a bearing on child and maternal health, have been prepared for the Department of National Health and Welfare by the national film board of Canada:
Films:
"Mother and Her Child"-based on the book "The Canadian Mother and Child" covers both the prenatal and postnatal phases and the care and development of the child up to one year of age.
"Know Your Baby"-illustrates proved methods of psychological care of the new-born infant.
"The Feeling of Rejection"-the first of a proposed series of films on mental mechanisms, designed to illustrate the development of personality factors which often lead to emotional difficulties and physical distress.
"Small Fry"-illustrates the provisions being made for the welfare of Canada's children,
pointing out improvements in education, diet and environment.
"Something to Chew On"-a film for parents showing the correct method of caring for children's teeth.
"Stanley Takes a Trip"-shows in entertaining cartoon fashion the' foods required by a normal growing boy.
Filmstrips:
"Nine to Get Ready"-covers the essential points in prenatal care to ensure the best possible start in life for babies.
"Introducing Baby"-gives detailed information on the care of mother and child from the time the baby is born until the weaning period.
"Internal Triangle"-a cartoon filmstrip describing the adventures of two teen-age girls with Canada's food rules.

speechtext: What steps have been taken by the venereal disease control division, Department of National Health and Welfare, to assist provinces in educating the public?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
1.	Early in 1947 the federal division of venereal disease control purchased 22 automatic filmstrip projectors at a cost of approximately $75 each. These were distributed to the provinces for display purposes. A general venereal disease educational filmstrip titled: "Protection Against V.D." was prepared in both English and French by the division and distributed among the provinces for use in the projectors. At present, two further filmstrips, one on syphilis and one on gonorrhoea, are in process of preparation. These are being designed along general public educational lines and will be in colour.

2.	A booklet (3,000 copies) dealing with the use of "Bal" as an anti-arsenical drug was prepared and distributed to the members of the medical profession.
3.	15,000 blotters titled: "Break the Chain of Infection" were produced for distribution among members of the medical profession. This blotter stressed the importance of reporting contacts.
4.	10,000 reprints of an article in Maclean's magazine by Michael Gardiner titled: "Our shameful Y.D. record" were purchased and distributed to the provinces.
5.	5,000 reprints of an article in the Canadian Home Journal by H. Cecil Rhodes titled: "What's the score on VX).?" were purchased and distributed to the provinces.
6.	10,000 reprints of the article in the Nursing Journal by Pearl Stiver titled, "They, too, are our patients", were purchased and distributed.
7.	The venereal disease platform presentation chart, for use by lecturers, was produced

Questions
and distributed to the provinces. Nearly a thousand of these were printed, in both English and French, durably bound, each consisting of 30 individual coloured charts, 18" x 30".
8.	Now being printed is a 65-page book titled: "Venereal disease-what you should know" which will have a dual function. It will serve as a guide for those using the V.D. platform presentation charts, and will be used as a comprehensive informational brochure for general lay education on the subject of V.D. The book carries a reproduction of the 30 charts on the lefthand pages with explanatory textual material on the opposite page. The initial printing order is for 12,000 English and 3,000 French copies.
9.	Now being printed is a series of six blotters dealing with various aspects of venereal disease educational material for lay distribution. These blotters are multicoloured and artistically designed to convey information with pictorial effectiveness. Each is aimed at a specific group: e.g., those contemplating marriage, teen-agers, expectant mothers, etc. The initial order is for 300,000 to be distributed to the provinces for use in their venereal disease control program.
10.	Approximately 6,000 venereal disease posters, for public display purposes, have been distributed to the provinces. These stress the importance of early treatment and pre-natal tests, warn against promiscuity, point out the dangers of neglect, etc.
11.	Miscellaneous pieces of venereal disease literature running into many thousands of copies (in addition to the particular projects listed above) were distributed through the department's information services division.
12.	Many thousand textbooks, pamphlets, etc. were obtained for the provinces directly from publishers by the federal division of venereal disease control.
Note 1: The above covers 1947 only. Two films "16 to 22" and "Very Dangerous" were adapted for general distribution in 1946.
Note 2: Most of the material produced for the provinces is sent out stamped with the provincial V.D. control department imprints, advising the public where they may obtain further information and advice.

BLINDNESS-RESTORATION OP SIGHT BY MEDICAL METHODS
speechtext:
1.	To what extent can the Department of National Health and Welfare control blindness?
2.	Is the said department taking any steps to inform the public that medical methods can restore adequate sight to a considerable number of blind persons?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: BLINDNESS-RESTORATION OP SIGHT BY MEDICAL METHODS
speechtext:
1.	Under the British North America Act responsibility in health matters is mainly that of the provincial and local governments, with the exception of the care of members of the armed services, veterans (under certain circumstances), Indians and Eskimos, immigrants upon their first arrival in Canada, and lepers. The Department of National Health and Welfare does not issue regulations designed to control and prevent blindness and the department cannot at present control blindness except by means of an educational campaign designed to inform the public of the causes and treatment of blindness and the medical means which can be taken to control and prevent blindness.
2.	The department informs the public by radio, by films and by various publications of methods to be used in the prevention and treatment of eye trouble and blindness.
The blindness control division has prepared two booklets, "Save Your Eyes" and "Eyestrain, its cause and treatment". These are being widely distributed through the provinces in French and English. The blindness control division shared in the cost of two educational films concerning the eyes. These are being showm on the national film board circuits and they have attracted large and appreciative audiences. The latest film had been seen by 121,629 persons by September, 1947. The blindness control division also supplied the minister with medical information which he incorporated in a radio address given on September 13, 1947, entitled "Clear vision for Canadians".
The blindness control division is engaged in research into the causes of blindness and its prevention and in the preparation of further publications of general interest to the public on eye conditions. A booklet is now in
Orders for Returns

course of preparation, for free distribution, on the subject of preventable blindness.
The blindness control division is keeping in touch with the -methods used in the control and treatment of blindness in other countries.
Funds have been voted by th-e dominion government to be used on a 75-25 per cent basis, in agreement with the provinces, to conduct a treatment scheme to determine whether an appreciable number of blind can be removed from the pension rolls by operation and medical treatment. This project has been endorsed twice by the deputy ministers of health as members of the dominion council of health. To date only the province of New Brunswick has passed an order in council providing for participation in this scheme, although lists of suitable cases are in the hands of the other provincial authorities.
