speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, March 16, consideration in committee of Bill No. 136, to amend the Continuation of Transitional Measures Act, 1947-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. W. MAYHEW (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to enlarge upon the brief statement I made in the house on the evening of March 16, with regard to the Canadian Sugar Stabilization
Corporation Limited, and to reply to some of the questions asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and the hon. member for Rosedale.
The Canadian Sugar Stabilization Corporation Limited, as I said on that evening, was incorporated as a crown company in March, 1947, to take over the duties and responsibilities which previously had been vested in the sugar administrator of the wartime prices and trade board. I stated that the corporation had acquired or is acquiring Canada's 1948 requirements of imported cane sugar. I was asked if bulk buying was desirable in peace or was continued only when necessary. It is the policy of the board, under the direction of the government, to withdraw from bulk purchasing as soon as it ceases to be necessary in the public interest. In October 1939 an agreement was entered into with the government of the United Kingdom on a plan of co-ordinating the purchasing of sugar for the duration of the war and for such period thereafter as might be considered necessary to permit of return to normal trading. This agreement was eventually embodied in an exchange of notes in September 1940. In the autumn of 1945 the United Kingdom intimated that they proposed, in the interests of maximum production and an orderly return to normal trade, to guarantee the purchase of all empire cane sugar to the end of 1949, and inquired whether Canada would wish to participate in these purchase arrangements. After full and careful discussion we agreed to participate up to our import requirements, with the proviso that we could withdraw at any time preceding the opening of the new crop year if we felt the proposed prices were too high.
Our present position is that we are in this arrangement for 1948, and that we have the right to withdraw from the 1949 crop at any time prior to December, 1948, if we feel that the proposed price for 1949 is too high. It was then and still is our view that our average price for 1947,	1948 and 1949
under this agreement would be below the average free market price for those years. The world sugar supply, up to and including the 1948 crops, was allocated through the international emergency food council. The 1948 crops are not under international allocation. We agreed with the United Kingdom, however, early in the summer of 1947 that we would buy our 1948 requirements of non-empire sugars from the United Kingdom ministry of food, paying their actual average costs.
We are informed that the highest price paid for 1948 sugar by the United Kingdom
Transitional Measures Act

under these arrangements is $5 per hundred pounds, and the lowest price is $3.75. The agreed price for the 1948 empire cane sugar is $4.75. The average price for all sugar purchased appears likely to be about $4.81. The market quotations for sugar for the 1948 crop have been as high as $5.25 and as low as $3.65. The present open market price is about 84.15. All these prices are f.o.b. West Indies islands. The duty on empire sugar is 29 cents per hundred pounds and on foreign sugar $1.29 per hundred pounds. It is estimated that about 50 per cent of the 1948 imports will come from empire sources and 50 per cent from non-empire sources. The continuance of the Canadian sugar stabilization corporation is necessary to give effect to these arrangements relating to sugar, at least until the 1948 purchase program is completed. The corporation's present selling price to refineries is on the basis of $5.94 per hundred pounds of raw sugar of 96 degree polarization. The refiners' maximum price for refined sugar is $7.89 net per hundred pounds f.o.b. Montreal.
Then I thought the committee would be interested in these figures, which I am able to give. The estimated sugar requirements for Canada for the year is 600,000 tons, of which 250,000 tons is estimated to come from empire sources, 150,000 tons from Santo Domingo, about 100,000 tons from other foreign sources, principally Cuba, and about 100,000 tons from our own domestic sugar beet producers.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I believe this raises the question whether or not this committee is in favour of bulk buying. Sufficient information has not been adduced to the committee to convince one that we are much better off by reason of this contract with Great Britain than we would be if we stood on our own feet and bought sugar where that could be done to the best advantage. For example, the present price of sugar is $4.15 per hundred pounds, while I understood the parliamentary assistant to say that at the present time we are paying an average price of about $4.81. These controls may seem good from certain points of view, but it is surprising how they may have repercussions which are not expected. Last October or November, for instance, I was in Regina and went through a warehouse where I saw carton after carton of American biscuits. Right across the road from this warehouse was the plant of a Canadian biscuit manufacturer. The thing seemed so peculiar that I asked the reason for it. I found that the wholesaler could not get enough Canadian biscuits because at that time I understood we were on a sugar ration or sugar quota;

so we were using our valuable United States dollars to import biscuits which, because of their sugar content, we did not have in Canada, though right next door to this warehouse was a biscuit manufacturer.
I do not profess to know all the ramifications of the sugar business, or of the biscuit business for that matter, but when you see a situation like that you immediately come to the conclusion that those who impose controls upon us little know just how far their controlling goes. Here we faced a situation where the most vital thing in our economy was the preservation of United States exchange. The United States had no sugar quota; it dealt in a free market in sugar, apparently, though I understand it left the empire countries to Great Britain. The United States had all the sugar they wanted; they had it for export in manufactured form, giving employment to her own people, while we were losing the small balance of exchange we had.
I do not understand why we in Canada have been kept on a quota longer than the United States. It may have something to do with the empire agreements, but I think it should be explained to the committee. I believe we would all be interested in learning what were the real advantages; whether or not the advantages outweigh the disadvantages of getting back to free enterprise and the purchase of sugar in the cheapest market we can find.
Just in passing, I happened to notice on the order paper today a question which was not answered. It was sent in by the hon. member for Lake Centre, who asked why we paid more for imported cane sugar than we paid our own growers of sugar beets. I think that question should be answered; it is part and parcel of this whole matter.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is another matter I wish to speak about.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is there no answer to what I have just said? I do not think the government has made out any case at all for the continuance of this contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is made for 1948.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The contract is made for 1948.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: When was it made?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In 1947. At the time it was made it looked like a good deal, and it may yet turn out to be even better than it looks at the present time. Sugar is bound to fluctuate from time to time; and I would suggest to the hon. gentleman and the committee that from the general appearance of

Transitional Measures Act
things it might be advisable to continue the arrangement for a time. But I can assure hon. members that it is the intention, to do away with this just as soon as possible, and it is possible that it may be done away with before the 1949 agreement comes into effect.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the agreement for 1948 was made in 1947, when in 1947 was it made? I should like to know when we shall consider the 1949 contract. It may be that it is almost due for consideration now, and the opinion of the committee may be useful.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I may be permitted to reinforce the question which has been asked. As the hon. member for Rosedale has said, today we have just been given a statement that the government considered it desirable to do this; I do not think we have been given any reason. This seems to me to leave the matter in an unsatisfactory^ position. I shall not press the point unduly, but inasmuch as the parliamentary assistant has stated virtually that this is the last year-or am I putting too much into what he says?-are we astute to get as much sugar as we can from sources other than dollar countries? We still seem to be buying a great deal there, a procedure which seems undesirable if it can be avoided.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Our present position is that we have entered into these arrangements for 1948, and we have a right to withdraw from the 1949 crop at any time prior to December 1948. Unless there be a development of some things we cannot now foresee, it looks to me as though we would be in a position to get out of this by the end of the coming fall.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not a question only of whether we are in a position to withdraw. My colleague asked whether it was the present intention of the government to withdraw.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I can assure the committee that it is the desire to get out of these arrangements as soon as possible. But it would be impossible to give the committee a definite date on which that will be done.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question supplementary to that of the hon. member for Rosedale. What was the determining factor which entered into the making of the contract? Was it a matter of quantity, or of price? While I realize that the factor of quantity may have been important during the war, I am more concerned about the trade relations which could be established between this country and some other producing countries. In years gone by we enjoyed a happy trade relationship with both Cuba and Santo 5849-150
Domingo. I should like to see these trade relations revived as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Both factors were considered-regard for a stable price and continuity of supply. Then, I believe I did give the figures when I pointed out that we will be purchasing about 150,000 tons from Santo Domingo and about 100,000 tons from other foreign sources, chiefly Cuba.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Was the price fixed when the contract was given, or is it a price based upon the market?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: For the empire sugar the British fix the price and we agree. For the non-empire sugar it will be the average price paid.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the average price lower than the British contract price?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the question is answered let me say that I am impressed by the distinction drawn, between empire and non-empire sugars. Non-empire sugar is imported direct from Cuba, while empire sugar must cross the ocean twice, both eastward and westward, before we get it. That is why it is so expensive.
Why should there be a sugar trust in London? Why should we be obliged to buy that sugar from London when we could have it direct from the West Indies? Not only that, but I renew the suggestion I have made before, that we are entitled to have part of the British empire. Why do we not have the West Indies? Everything has been given to everyone else; but when it comes to Canada we are too proud either to accept or to ask for anything. This is an example of one of the necessities coming from a tropical climate. In Canada we have no tropical temperatures and, while we have beet sugar, we do not have cane sugar. If the West Indies were transferred to Canada we would have cheaper sugar and would be able to import it direct. Why should there be so much red tape in trade? That red tape is paid for by the consumer. Is there anyone who loves the empire so much that he will be content to pay more dearly for his sugar? Where does the money go? It goes for maritime freight, and* to the owners of' the bottoms which carry the sugar both ways across the ocean. It is a fine trip for the sugar, and I am wondering if salt water improves its quality. I am told that if a keg of beer is put on a sailing vessel during the summer and permitted to remain there while the vessel is on a long voyage, it gives a certain gusto to the beer. I wonder if the same applies to sugar?
Transitional Measures Act

This is the kind of trade I denounce, not because it is trade within the empire but because it is nonsensical. Not only that, but we have to pay for it. The empire imports which we take are paid for from the advances we make to them. Couldi anything be sillier? That kind of trade cannot be justified. I was right when I denounced it two years ago this spring; and I am right again today when I suggest the government should be bold enough to tell the British government that it is time for Canada to have some of the crumbs from the British empire.
We are entitled to have the West Indies. I wonder if the government does not dare to ask for them from Great Britain because of the possibility of some objection from the United States. What business is it of the United States to interfere with our dealings with the old country? It is none of their business; it is our own. We are not an enemy country; rather we are a friendly country. There is no great wall of China between the United States and Canada-and how many times have I heard that repeated!
I suggest that we should have sensible, practical and realistic trade with all parts of the world. As I have said, we do not have a tropical climate in Canada; therefore let us have a part of the empire which is in a tropical zone. We might have visits from English warships at times, if we were to own the West Indies. Nevertheless we are entitled to have them, after all the sacrifice in men, money and food, and sacrifices of all descriptions, we have made for the empire.
I may be called an isolationist when I suggest that, but I am not an isolationist. I follow the practice of practical English businessmen and the example of the English bulldog who tries to get all he can for his country. That is laudable. Why should we not follow that example? Why are we so subservient? When we import sugar why should we pay freight on a double crossing of the ocean? That has to be paid for by the Canadian consumer, who has a heavy enough burden to bear already. I know very well that the matter will not be taken into consideration now, but I am throwing out suggestions in order that members of parliament will have an opportunity to think about them and to realize that Canada is entitled to her share of the British empire before it goes somewhere else. Already Palestine has gone; Egypt has gone. Let us at least save the West Indies for Canada. They will be much better off with us than with any other country in the world.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Ternis-couata is sound in his argument in regard to

freight rates, I suggest to the minister and his officials that they give serious thought to basing the price on an Atlantic coast port where raw sugar is landed instead of on Montreal. As it is now, it looks to me as though once again central Canada is being given protection. The price is based on* Montreal, in central Canada. We pay the freight on the raw product to Montreal to be refined there and then shipped to other parts of Canada. I say the price should be based on the Atlantic coast port where the sugar is landed. I am glad to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce here. This is an opportunity for him and other members of the cabinet to give encouragement to Nova Scotia and the maritimes by insisting that the Acadia Sugar Refinery be reopened for the refining of sugar, thus producing sugar on the Atlantic coast more cheaply and bringing down the cost to the consumers throughout the whole dominion.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If I may be permitted one word more, according to correspondence which I receive from people living in the West Indies and from what I hear from friends who go there, the public feeling in the West Indies is that it should join up with Canada. A large proportion of the population in Trinidad, Jamaica and the other islands wish to do so, and if the question were put to a vote they would join up with Canada at once.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Temiscouata is quite wrong in saying that the sugar crosses the ocean twice. It comes direct from the islands to Canada. As a matter of fact we are paying for empire sugar approximately $4.75 and for foreign sugar $4.87. The British have purchased all the exportable surplus on the islands and they are selling it to us at their cost. Landed in Saint John, New Brunswick, it is two cents per hundredweight less than when landed in Montreal. Sugar prices are based on Saint John, Montreal and Vancouver, at the same price.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why not include Halifax? I have nothing against Saint John, but for years we had the Acadia Sugar Refinery operating. During the war it was closed down because, we were told, of a shortage of fuel oil. I think that this is an opportunity for the government to step into the picture and once again have the Acadia Sugar Refinery at Woodside resume operations, which would also provide badly needed employment in that part of the country and once again make Woodside, a suburb of Dartmouth, a prosperous community.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halifax will appreciate that it was not by action of

Transitional Measures Act
the dominion government that that refinery was closed down. I do not know exactly what he is suggesting now. Is it that we quote a low price for raw sugar at a place where there is not a refinery?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. I go beyond that. I say that here is an opportunity for the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the cabinet, including the highly-respected minister representing Nova Scotia, to help the maritimes by taking action which will result in the re-opening of the Acadia Sugar Refinery at Woodside. It was closed down during the war because of a shortage of fuel oil, or at all events that was the reason given at the time- that it was a war casualty. Of course it may have been just another manoeuvre on the part of the promotors to centralize the refining of sugar. In any case I am asking the government to take action which will result in the re-opening of the Acadia Sugar Refinery.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member and the minister a question? Does it not follow that he is really asking the government to open up and operate that refinery as a government proposition?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No; you cannot put me in that position.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You are putting yourself there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. If I see a man who needs help, who needs a meal, for instance, I am glad to help him, as I am sure my hon. friend would. The government is perhaps in a position to assist those who formerly operated the Acadia Sugar Refinery.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: This is not my department, but I could not imagine the government refusing to give a Halifax buyer of raw sugar as low a price as the Saint John buyer. It is based on the West Indies price, plus freight, and the freight is less to Saint John than to Montreal. If there is a refinery in Halifax the freight to that port would be less than to Montreal.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The only price quoted by the parliamentary assistant in his first statement, before I had spoken, was based on Montreal. I still feel that the government could do something.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We could certainly do that.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: A by-election?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I very seldom think of politics.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I ask the parliamentary assistant why the Minister of Finance persists in refusing to grant the request of the sugar 5849-150i
beet growers to have the price of sugar produced from beets equalized with that of sugar produced from cane? At present there is a spread of 19 cents on the average, from $7.89 to $8.08. The sugar beet growers have consistently asked that the government pay the same price for sugar from sugar beets as for sugar from imported cane. The government maintain that they are not subsidizing sugar, or that they will not subsidize sugar producers in this country, but if they are subsidizing, as they really are, cane sugar importations to the extent of 19 cents a hundred I do not see why the sugar beet growers do not get the same consideration, the same price f.o.b. at Montreal. It has never been satisfactorily explained to the sugar beet growers so far as I know, and I should like to have an answer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am advised that traditionally beet sugar has been lower than cane sugar, but some time ago beet sugar was raised to the same price as cane sugar. If Montreal is the base, then the price in the sugar factory in Winnipeg would be that price plus the freight; therefore the beet sugar growers in Manitoba would get the Montreal price plus the freight from Montreal to Winnipeg.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps you can say that in one way, but is it not a fact that the cane sugar people are getting another 19 cents a hundred? You may be paying it out of your $21,000,000 stabilization fund, but actually the cane sugar people are getting 19 cents a hundred more at Montreal than the sugar beet growers; that is, on the basis f.o.b. Montreal. It does not matter where the money comes from; the cane sugar producers are getting the benefit, to the extent of 19 cents a hundred, over the sugar beet growers.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Just a word on the information given by the parliamentary assistant; he said that the non-British sugar was more expensive than the British sugar; that there was a difference of 12 cents. That may be so, but he knows very well that there are fluctuations in the price of such commodities. Today the difference is on one side; tomorrow it may be on the other side. But taking into account these fluctuations, it is more than evident that it would be to the benefit of Canada to have the West Indies as part of Canada. They are nearer to Nova Scotia than the part of the country in which I live. Everybody would be satisfied to have the West Indies as part of Canada. If that came about we could get sugar, molasses, bananas, rum and all the products of tropical countries from these islands, and it would come from our own country to the great satisfaction of all.
Transitional Measures Act

Another thing I notice is that these are dealings between governments. If I am not mistaken these purchases are made between governments. I wonder whether that is so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Just a minute. I have asked a question. I wonder whether the commercial exchanges are between representatives of both governments, both exporters. I should like to know whether, when we buy empire sugar, it is bought through the British government or from private firms in these countries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The British government actually purchases the sugar and we are buying it at their cost. Our cheques actually are paid to the growers, not to the British government. That probably answers the hon. gentleman's question. If I understood the hon. member aright he said that empire sugar was costing more than foreign sugar. That is not so. The reverse is true.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I understand, and I admit what my hon. friend has said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We do not know what the fluctuation is going to be, and the contract is for only 1948. What might happen in 1949 is something else.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In the first part of my remarks I said that empire sugar was more expensive, and in the second part I took into account what my hon. friend has said. I notice that there is a difference of 12 cents, and that non-empire sugar is more expensive; but I was under the impression that both governments were dealing together in the purchase of that sugar. That would be pure socialism, and the cost would not have been the same at all concerning the purchase of non-empire sugar. I am glad that my hon. friend has said that the British government was making the arrangement but that payment was made directly to the producers. I congratulate them, and I warn them to be very careful in their dealings with Mr. Strachey, because he does not keep his word very often.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want to add a word. I think we cannot pretend that the explanation which has been given as to why this was done takes us very far. The statement has been made that it was thought wise to do so. One wonders whether it has just been continued without anyone standing off and criticizing it. I am looking at it in a detached way to consider whether the time has not come to get away from bulk buying; nevertheless I am not disposed to follow the

matter further, but I should like to say this. I hope very earnestly that it will not be necessary to continue it beyond this year. There has been considerable indication from the parliamentary assistant that it may not go further, although he has not bound himself. If it comes up again we of this party will certainly be very critical, and we shall try to resist any further extension of it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like an answer to my question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I can see the parliamentary assistant's point but our difficulty is that the sugar beet growers, and the sugar beet company in Manitoba anyway, feel that if the government would meet the request of the

Transitional Measures Act
sugar beet growers and equalize prices, cutting out the 19 cent disparity, it would increase acreage. It would be of advantage to Canada and would help the dollar situation if sugar beet acreage were increased. If however we wait until the particular item to which the parliamentary assistant has referred is brought down, it will be too late even then, if nothing is done about it before that time, to encourage an increase in acreage which should be sown in 1948. That is why I would like to have the parliamentary assistant discuss it with the Minister of Finance. Perhaps the minister could even yet adjust what the sugar beet growers claim is a great injustice.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The matter will be discussed with the ministry.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wish to say a word of appreciation of the Minister of Finance and the parliamentary assistant for their willingness to answer so many questions on so many different subjects. These matters are delicate and difficult and they do their best to inform the house. I am sure everyone has appreciated the way in which they have dealt with the questions that have been submitted to them. The answers were mostly satisfactory to members.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant to answer the question I asked on Tuesday, which he deferred to a later day? The question had reference to whether or not a directive had been issued to the rental commissioners to favour the tenant rather than the owner of property. He said he would give the answer some time later. I am concerned about the answer because I have received many letters from veterans and old folks who own homes and are unable to obtain occupancy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There has been no directive issued by the board along the lines suggested.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There hasn't been any?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I wonder if we might revert to the discussion of the other evening on the two orders in council listed under the Department of Mines and Resources, 7167 and 7168. The other night I asked a question about these orders in council and the Minister of Trade and Commerce was good enough to make an immediate reply which took the form of an announcement as to the change that had been made in government policy with regard to this matter. Incidentally I have to point out that one of the difficulties in connection with this kind of
legislation is this. When we passed the bill a year ago it carried forward a number of orders in council. Some of these we were opposed1 to and yet they have been carried forward another year, while other orders in council like these we were in favour of, and had1 hoped would be continued, have been revoked in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I interrupt to say that when the two orders in council referred to were extended last year I gave notice that it would be only a matter of a short time until they would no longer be required. At that time I expressed the government's viewpoint that minerals in the ground should1 not be subject to control.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I can confirm that the minister gave that indication when the matter was up last year, but I still press the view that these orders in council should have been continued, or that the provisions brought into effect by these orders should have been made effective by permanent statute. It is obvious to all of us that we are at a very early stage in this whole matter of radioactive minerals and atomic energy. It seems to me, in view of the losses that the Canadian people have sustained in the past from the alienation of raw materials and natural resources, we should go rather slowly in this new field of atomic energy.
I remember the Minister of Trade and Commerce telling us on another occasion that he did not want to see a repetition of the experiences that this country suffered in the matter of railroading. He did not want to see those experiences repeated in air transportation. We take the same position with respect to radioactive minerals and atomic energy.
I say as briefly and as pointedly as I can that we disagree with the minister. We feel that these minerals should have been reserved to the crown, at least until the world knows a little more about this subject. It is interesting to note the sort of publicity that has been given to this announcement and the items that have been in the news in the last day or two. This morning's radio carried the news that gold miners were now turning their attention to uranium rather than to gold. Maybe we shall not have to go ahead with Bill No. 7, in which the hon. member for York West and others are so interested, now that this guaranteed price has been fixed for uranium concentrates, with the understanding that the government will buy all the uranium concentrates of a certain specification that are produced.
Transitional Measures Act

In view of the fact that we do not yet know how fully these minerals will be used either for war or for peace, I suggest that we are opening the door to a new phase of profiteering, and I feel very strongly that this alienation of yet another natural resource should not have been permitted by the federal government. I realize that the present policy-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: What resource is being alienated? I would point out that any and all uranium mined in this country must be sold to the federal government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am coming to that immediately. Radioactive minerals in the ground, by the orders in council that have been revoked, were reserved to the crown even while in the ground. Now the government has moved to the position that private interests may go in and explore and exploit and develop these minerals, though the minister points out that the government maintains its control in this field by buying all the uranium that is produced.
That is the position at the present time, but I ask hon. members to note that it is a change from what it was before, and I also ask hon. members to note the quotation which the minister gave the other night from a memorandum he had just received with regard to the position in the United States. On page 2285 of Hansard will be found this quotation with reference to the policy of the atomic energy commission in the United States:
In general it will be commission policy to purchase ores for its program from private sources and limit direct government production as far *as possible.
I have not before me the details of the United States program, either as at the present time or for the future, but that sentence sug-gets to me that the commission in the United States thinks in terms of private interests having stockpiles of this material from which the United States atomic energy commission will purchase supplies for its program. The minister said the other night that although arrived at independent!}-, this government and the United States government were following somewhat parallel lines. I should not be surprised if before long the minister announced a further change of policy that permits this sort of thing, namely, the stockpiling of these materials by private interests. The very fact that the government purchases uranium from private interests means that there is a stage at which private interests own this material. It is obvious to all of us that there is no way of telling what the value of these materials will be. I think it is a little too soon for action of this kind to have been taken. In

fact I would hope that we might move in the direction that this sort of action would never have to be taken. But at least in the present situation I regret that the government has taken this stand.
I do not think I shall say anything more at this moment, but will merely ask a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The statement he made the other night related, I take it, to these two orders in council that have been revoked. They referred only to the radioactive minerals in the Yukon and in the Northwest Territories. That is natural because those are the only parts of Canada in which the natural resources belong to the crown in the right of the federal government. Can the minister tell us what the situation is in the rest of Canada? I refer to the provinces. I realize that that matter is not under his jurisdiction, but it is one of general interest. Can the minister tell us what the situation is in the various provinces?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Before the minister answers that question, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. How does he suggest that the prospecting for these precious metals be carried out? Does he really believe that the government can prospect for minerals and find them in just as many cases as individual Canadians can?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Individual Canadians can do the prospecting, but they can do it now. just as they did while these orders in council were in effect, under the direction of the government and with the full knowledge that those minerals belong to the government. We have had this sort of discussion a good many times before, and hon. members to my right need not think that what we are saying is any criticism of the rights of individual mining prospectors. They are Canadians; they are workers like a good many more, and deserve their chance to make a decent living. The thing that bothers me is that it is not the individual prospector who makes a mint of money out of mining; it is organizations like Eldorado before it became a crown corporation, Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, and so on. Frankly I have no confidence in organizations of that kind when it comes to a subject which is so tremendous in its energy potential and its wealth-producing potential, not to mention its relation to the problem of war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not answered my question. Does he really believe that these minerals can be found best by employees of any government, whether dom-

Transitional Measures Act
inion or provincial? Or does he believe they can be found best by companies, let us say, or individuals whose business is prospecting?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In reply to that question I would say that most of the prospecting that is done today is done with all kinds of help that comes from governments, both federal and provincial. If it were not for all the assistance to mining, such as geodetic surveying and all the rest of it, that is afforded through the expenditure of public money, the prospectors would have a tough time of it.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. member does not know much about mining.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Does the minister expect to increase the amount of uranium ore found in Canada by this recent lifting of the government restriction?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: To answer to the first question first, the federal government, as my hon. friend has said, owns the ore only in the Northwest Territories. The provinces own the natural resources within their boundaries. When the ban on prospecting for uranium was imposed by the federal government, each province was communicated with and asked to put into effect a similar prohibition in the provinces. I think seven of the provinces did that and two did not. I leave it to my hon. friend to guess which two did not.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is no difficulty there.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: As soon as it was felt that it was no longer necessary for the crown to control uranium, the provinces were notified accordingly; and I think all the provinces except Saskatchewan have taken parallel action with the dominion in lifting the prohibition against prospecting. To reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Trinity, yes, we think that opening up uranium prospecting will increase the known reserves of uranium. As hon. gentlemen know, there are in this country a good many million miles of suitable territory to be explored. The federal government for these three years have had a number of parties out-I think some twenty or twenty-two-and certain discoveries have been made. The value of the discoveries cannot be determined until they are opened up. We think that with all the prospectors who are looking for other minerals but are also on the lookout for uranium and those who may be sent out to look primarily for uranium, there will be further discoveries.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Has the status of Eldorado changed as a result of your orders?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No. Eldorado is a mining property at Great Bear lake. They are operating a refinery at Port Hope. They are also opening up one or two prospects that have been discovered in the last year or two. But Eldorado is most active and we are hoping its activities will be stepped up as the result of the new regulation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Has the minister ever tabled the report of the investigation into Eldorado?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not know of any investigation into Eldorado.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was brought up by way of question last year and the year before. I have reference to the report of the Glassco commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That was an interdepartmental report. It will not be tabled.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I disagree with the government's policy in this respect. I think it is wrong. But unfortunately the whole situation concerning this valuable mineral and what we derive from it is shrouded in secrecy, and perhaps with good reason. Today, however, I intend to ask the minister some questions and I hope to get an answer to most of them. None of them will affect security matters at all. The right hon. gentleman, in this statement of his the other day, either said too much or too little; but he has left a great many x's in the equation and I should like to hear the answers to them.
In the first place I should like to lay a background for what I have to say by quoting from the official United States report on atomic energy, with which the minister is well acquainted. The author in his preface states:
The ultimate responsibility for our nation's policy rests on its citizens and they can discharge such responsibilities wisely only if they are informed.
I shall go right to the end and quote words from this book which I think every member of parliament should read. They are found at page 135:
We find ourselves with an explosive which is far from completely perfected. Yet the future possibilities of such explosives are appalling, and their effects on future wars and international affairs are of fundamental importance. Here is a new tool for mankind, a tool of unimaginable destructive power. Its development raises many questions that must be answered in the near future. Because of the restrictions of military security there has been no chance for the congress or the people to debate such questions.
Such, of course, is obviously true in Canada as well, to some extent.
They have been seriously considered by all concerned and vigorously debated among the
Transitional Measures Act

scientists, and the conclusions reached have been passed along to the highest authorities. These questions are not technical questions; they are political and social questions, and the answers given to them may affect all mankind for generations.
We may have to bring up some of these questions in this house, in the hope of getting answers. The report goes on:
In thinking about them the men on the project have been thinking as citizens of the United States vitally interested in the welfare of the human race.
Again we could substitute "Canada" for "the United States".
It has been their duty and that of the responsible high government officials who were informed to look beyond the limits of the present war and its weapons to the ultimate implications of these discoveries. This was a heavy responsibility. In a free country like ours such questions should be debated by the people and decisions must be made by the people through their representatives.
We now have an opportunity, though brief, to discuss some of the fundamental issues contained in the statement made by the minister the other day. The policy of the government is avowedly to permit private exploration for and mining of radioactive materials. As I say, I disagree with that policy just now, because I do not agree with those who see in this new substance, fissionable material, a way to open up suddenly vast resources of energy and potential wealth for the people of the nations. We may not see that in our lifetime; but I am convinced of this, that as far as the nations of the world are concerned, the real value of atomic energy today lies in its power to destroy, to kill and to obliterate. This means we have to consider the policy of the government from that point of view; and that policy is to permit, to some extent, so-called private enterprise-I suppose because the government considers it more efficient- to profit out of this material which is so extraordinarily dangerous when it reaches the end stage.
I should like to have seen the government continue its policy of maintaining title, in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, to these radioactive materials; and I should like to see the government continue the agreement with the provinces, as far as possible. I believe the provinces should be asked to work in co-operation with the federal government, so that when such radioactive minerals are found in the provinces they can be exploited in conjunction with the federal government for the benefit of all.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
If the hon. member will permit a question, is he prepared to see the prov-

inces and the dominion spend the taxpayers' money on the exploration and development of such deposits?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is already being spent. We have spent thousands and probably hundreds of thousands of dollars in that way. I have no objection to that, because this material is one of the most vital things in the world today. We have to look at it from that aspect, and from no other. In his statement at page 2284 of Hansard, the minister said:
The government will purchase . . . acceptable uranium bearing ores . . .
Here begins my list of questions. The minister said such ores must have a minimum uranium content equivalent to ten per cent by weight of uranium oxide. What will be the position with respect to ores containing only five per cent of uranium oxide, say, or seven and a half per cent, or eight per cent, or nine per cent? Does the government intend to purchase all such ores, or will it leave the ores with a lesser uranium oxide content in the hands of those doing the mining? If so, what will be the consequences of that policy from the point of view of stock-piling, with which I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre dealt cogently?
That is one question. On the next I admit my ignorance and would be glad to be guided by the minister. What about the question of thorium? The Prime Minister told us in this house some two years ago that thorium was a basic necessity for the manufacture of atomic bombs; yet there is no mention of it here at all. I should like the minister to say something about that.
Then in the statement by the minister we are told that a minimum rate of $2.75 a pound will be paid for this ore. The question which immediately arises in my mind is this. Is $2.75 a pound an excessive price to pay, or is it a reasonable price? We can be certain that the price is not too low, but I should like to know whether the price of $2.75 a pound gives a reasonable return to those who are producing this ore. Who determined that price? On what basis was it determined? Was it done by the department itself, or was it done by the government in conjunction with the corporations which will mine this substance? That is another matter I should like to know something about.
There is something else we must remember. In 1939 an agreement was entered into between the Eldorado company and Union Miniere du Haut Katanga, which was the Belgian company working in the Congo. These two companies were in the field to develop radium, and they had come to the conclusion that if they carried

Transitional Measures Act
on production at the rate then in effect the price would have to be dropped. So they entered into this agreement, under which the Belgian company was to get sixty per cent of the market and the Canadian company, forty per cent. As an annual mining review stated, they did this because the developed potential exceeded absorption capacity. Radium is one of the most vital materials we know of for the preservation of health, for the prevention of disease and, through that prevention, the preservation of life; yet no matter how great the need among the peoples of the world, these two companies decided at that time to restrict production. The reason for that may have been, in the words of the United' States statement which was quoted by the minister, "under the stimulus of profits," but I regret very much to see the stimulus of profits used in such a way. What guarantee is there that this sort of agreement will not be entered into in future? The minister has stated that he looks with approval upon United States policy; but then United States policies have not the complete support of United States scientists and public men. Here I should like to quote part of a study made for a seminar in government administration and public policy at Harvard University, by Mr. Richard Dyer McCann, who is a lecturer there. He said:
Government operation is only partly envisaged in the atomic energy act of 1946. The "declaration of policy" in the act calls for "strengthening free competition in private enterprise" as well as a number of other objectives like increasing the standard of living, promoting world peace, and so on. The accompanying committee report stated that "wherever possible, the committee endeavours to reconcile government monopoly of fissionable material with our tradi-tionable free enterprise system."
Some observers say that under Republican tutelage, atomic energy will be completely "returned" to private enterprise.
That is the hope of many in the United States today. It may even be the aspiration of some in Canada; but as far as I am concerned, it is our responsibility in this party to see that, as far as we can avoid it, that does not become Canada's policy, and I hope it does not. The effects of such a policy can be seen in a later quotation from the same article:
General Electric now has responsibility for a huge new research laboratory at Schenectady and has taken over from duPont the Hanford works in Washington-by far the most important of the three production plants.
That is one of the largest plants erected by the United States government for the manufacture of fissionable material.
Thus General Electric becomes the primary wholesaler of atomic power. Gan it be doubted that General Electric expects to have things
to say about the placement of secondary power plants in the United States? Can it be doubted therefore, that decisions about production policy of the united nations atomic energy commission -and of any future ADA-are of considerable importance ito General Electric? May it not be assumed that we are witnessing the conscious or unconscious growth of new, top-level lobbying interests, economic in character, international in scope?
I should like to be reassured by the minister that this will not be the policy of the federal government, namely, to turn this tremendous power for good and evil into private hands. While here again the facts are quite obscure, we know there were many suspicious, let us say, of what was happening in connection with certain officers of the Eldorado Mining Company some years ago.
How does the government intend, by a system of controls, to see to it that there are no illicit operations in the selling of uranium oxide? How will the government police this operation without, to some extent, leading to that police state which we all deplore? Would it not be better, in the long run, to take over complete ownership of these materials now, rather than be compelled to do so later if, unhappily, we find ourselves in another war?
It may seem to be the easier and more facile way out of the difficulty to have control now; but I think, in the long run, the problem will become much more complicated. I do not think we are doing a service to Canadians by allowing this stimulus of profit to decide how much ore will be produced. I assume we need the maximum amount of ore which can be produced in this country for defence if for no other reason. Yet today we leave its production entirely to the stimulus of profit.
I do not share the easy optimism of those who, as I said before, believe that, through atomic energy', a new world is just around the corner. On the other hand I am inclined to share the pessimism of those who know what an atomic war would mean to the people of the world. And it is because I fear that eventuality that I should like to see entire control of all fissionable material and by-products, from their original source, in the hands of the federal government.
On December 17, 1945, as reported at page 3703 of Hansard, when discussing the atomic energy declaration the Prime Minister said:
If we are agreed on the ultimate necessity of some measure of world government to maintain world security, we should, by every means in our power, support and strengthen every agency of international co-operation and understanding which can help to make the world community a reality.
2360
Transitional Measures Act

I think that, in this small action of the government, it has denied the words of the Prime Minister. Had the government been alive to the moral responsibility which it had to the people, of Canada and of the world, it would have said to the united nations, "We are willing to transfer to any international organization the plant which we have in Canada for the production of fissionable materials, and also to surrender to that international organization the areas in which there are quantities of uranium oxide." There, at least, would have been a gesture of some value to a world which is becoming almost paralyzed with fear. It would have been the type of moral leadership which is badly needed; but the government is falling down on it. It may be suggested from the Social Credit group that this would be a surrender of sovereignty. Of course it is. We cannot expect to live any longer as a sovereign nation; and in any event I doubt very much whether this sovereignty we boast of is a reality or is indeed a myth.
Here again I quote from the Prime Minister from the same page in Hansard:
The more deeply one ponders the problems with which our world is confronted in the light -"the terrible light," as Mr. Attlee said-of the implications of the development of atomic energy, the harder it is to see a solution in anything short of some surrender of national sovereignty.
Of course that is the answer in the long run. But I think the government has made an egregious blunder in carrying out its policy. Perhaps time will tell whether I am right or wrong. But in the meantime, at least I wish to register my opposition to this policy, and to hope that the minister will be able to answer some of the questions T have raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The first question, I think, w'as as to the significance of the ten per cent content. That refers entirely to the degree of concentration of the ore which is offered for delivery. Eldorado ore is very low grade. It runs less than one per cent, and is concentrated to about thirty per cent. The government has specified ten per cent as the degree of concentration which it will expect before it can accept delivery. Otherwise it has no significance.
Then, so far as thorium is concerned, may I point out that thorium is covered by atomic energy control. There is no known deposit of thorium in Canada. It is known mostly in tropical countries. The greatest supply is in India and the next is in Brazil.
As to the price of $2.75 a pound, it is felt that a price should be stated which would govern for a considerable length of time, so

that prospectors would be encouraged, and would have some method of assessing the value of any discoveries they made. The price of $2.75 was worked out from the experience of Eldorado as a reasonable price for that purpose.
Then, my hon. friend has referred to prewar agreements between Eldorado-that is the privately owned Eldorado-and	the
Belgian company. I would ask him to remember that the entry of the Canadian company into the field of the production of radium cut the price of radium in two. I think there was for a time a selling agreement between the two countries, but certainly there was no selling agreement after the government acquired the company, and there will be none in the future.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Has General McNaugh-ton been consulted regarding this policy? I have before me recommendations and reports presented with respect to the proposed atomic energy commission. I notice that General McNaughton is quite specific in his reports which dealt with the agency's functions in relation to the location and the mining of ores. There was one section which impressed me when I read it some time ago, and I looked it up only a few minutes ago. I might say that this paper was prepared by General Andrew G. L. McNaughton of Canada, group leader; Professor Jacques Errera of Belgium; Captain Alvaro Alberto of Brazil; Doctor Bertrand Goldschmidt of France; and Doctor John E. Vance of the United States.
This section struck me as significant:
Security requires international control and allocation of the quantities and locations of uranium and thorium separated from their deposit, time and place of processing and the size, use, and disposition of stocks. Without such comprehensive control of source materials there would be a serious risk of diversion or of the accumulation of stocks with a view to subsequent diversion or seizure. The policies governing this control must be specified in the convention. To administer them the agency must be given control of the source materials promptly after their separation from the deposits.
Therefore, agency ownership must apply to all uranium and thorium from the time of removal.
Reading the various reports made at the time by different persons-and this is mainly General McNaughton's summary-it struck me that, no matter how small the amount of uranium there might be in a concentrate, there would be danger of leakage if this were in the hands of private companies. I should like to see the government responsible for this all the way through.

Transitional Measures Act
Perhaps the minister could tell us whether what he proposes is satisfactory to our representative on the atomic energy commission of the united nations.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The two orders in council were revoked on recommendation of General Mc-Naughton, who was at that time chairman of the atomic energy board. Since that time, General McNaughton has assumed other duties and has resigned as president and member of the board. His place has been taken by Doctor Mackenzie of the national research council. But General McNaughton was chairman at the time this was rescinded.
If my hon. friend will read General Mc-Naughton's statement again he will notice that it recommends control of uranium from the time it is taken out of the ground. That is the purpose of the regulations, as first drawn, of the atomic energy commission. I explained a year ago, when the orders in council were extended, that it was the view of Canada that any attempt to control uranium in the ground was not useful, and that turned out to be the view of the atomic energy commission in New York. We are working in complete conformity with the findings of the commission, and we believe that the regulations- I have a copy of them here and I have no doubt my hon. friend has seen them-provide wholly adequate machinery for the control of uranium which is extracted from the ground.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I understand that this new move by the government comes as a result of consultation with a committee and others who are experts in the Canadian mining field and in atomic energy. I think the government has taken a wise and sensible step; in fact, almost the only step it could have taken under the circumstances. It has acted on the best technical and expert opinion available.
The problem before us in Canada is to see that all possible deposits of radioactive material are discovered and then developed. Whether we would like it or not, the fact remains that the government-and this goes for any government in a democracy-is not competent to discover and develop any ore deposit. One of the big problems of the geological survey is, as they put it, not to find a mine, because that is not their function. Their function is to make the geology so well known that the individual prospector, who has found well over ninety per cent of all the known mineral deposits in Canada today, will be able to discover and subsequently develop mineral deposits in this country. Incidentally when the Eldorado Mining and Smelting Company was taken over and the government's 5849-151J
policy made known at that time I advocated that the prospecting for and development of fissionable materials up to certainly the preliminary concentrate stage should be in the hands of those best able, in fact the only people able to discover and develop them, namely the individual prospector and the mining corporation. I am glad to see that the government has eventually come to that conclusion.
One of the things that this new move does is to put the Geiger counter into the kit of most prospectors. Today our knowledge of the fissionable materials in Canada is superficial. The discovery of the Eldorado deposit was in many ways a fluke. Gilbert LaBine at the time was looking for gold. The original Eldorado company was a gold mining company which had failed in operating a mine in Manitoba, I think it was; and it was only through Gilbert LaBine having a peculiar knowledge, a sort of sixth sense, which enabled him to detect a certain coloured stain on the ice of Great Bear lake that the Eldorado deposit was discovered. So it may be said that in many ways it was a fluke. If there are other deposits of uranium in Canada they are not known, and to prohibit the looking for these deposits and their development by individuals who are fortunate enough to discover them is not likely to lead to the discovery and development of more uranium deposits. It is essential that if there are other uranium deposits in Canada everything should be done to discover and develop them.
I think the government has taken the only sensible step in the circumstances. Whether the price is sufficient, no one in the house is competent to say. It would be difficult to say what the costs of concentrating U3O8 would1 be, and the government has set a price which is probably in the nature of a target price per pound. I hope that this will be considered a flexible price which may be varied to make possible and profitable the discovery of uranium or any other fissionable materials. There is, in my opinion and- in the opinion I think of the atomic energy commission, no danger in having these deposits discovered or in producing the concentrates of uranium so long as the end product continues to be controlled, and I understand from the committee in the United States that there is no idea that the end product shall in any way be released from the most stringent control by the federal authority.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I join with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Winnipeg North in protesting against the five-point program which the government
Transitional Measures Act

announced on March 16. Had I not been perfectly sure on other grounds that I was right in protesting against this policy, after listening to the Tory member to my right I am convinced I am right because we see that the government's policy is acceptable to him.
The development of atomic energy is still in its infancy. The success in breaking the atom so that it could be used for destructive purposes was heralded throughout the world as a discovery of equal importance to that of fire. Here we see a government right after the war, with the possibilities either of destruction or of peacetime use of that energy, ready to throw it into the hands of private enterprise where it will be promoted or retarded at the whim of such private enterprise. I take exception to that very principle because, for the good of the people of this country and for the good of the peoples throughout the world, I think we should undertake to develop atomic energy to its fullest. I cannot go so far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North and say that the peacetime uses of atomic energy may not come in our generation, I have read articles by well-known world scientists who hold the view that we may be able to use atomic energy in ten years. If we would go all-out and make an effort to use that energy for the welfare of the people we could find many uses for it in the matter of a few years.
Reference has already been made to the use of radioactive materials in determining certain functions in plant growth, and also in the field of medicine and surgery, where it is used to great advantage today. Therefore I want to register my great concern that this material be turned over to public enterprise to promote the development of it to the greatest extent possible. I should like to ask the minister whether the government has underwritten the production of all ore-bearing uranium oxide to the extent of $2.75 a pound. Will he tell the committee whether or not this is a low figure, and what is the possibility of a higher figure being paid? If a higher figure is paid in some instances, just how high is the government prepared to go? Here we have an instance of private companies going into exploratory work. They could very easily form a monopoly and hold back the production, thereby building up a sort of demand for it if the government should need it, and then request higher prices.
In conclusion may I say I feel that the government should reverse its program. Rather than attach our public development, or the development of these atomic uranium deposits to the skirts of the United States government, let us have our own policy and go all-out on public development.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Has the government any assurance that any claims staked by the private companies in developments of this kind will be developed? Is there any way in which the government is assured that the companies will not stake claims and then sit down on the job and keep other people from developing them?
