maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, there is no such assurance, except that it is very expensive to keep claims under control. My hon. friend knows that a certain amount of development work is required to keep title to a claim alive.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is there any regulation providing that anything that is produced in these mines must be delivered to the government immediately, or is there an opportunity for stock-piling?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It must be delivered immediately.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It seems to be the time to give some expression on this matter which is very important. We must consider it seriously. The minister holds Jupiter's thunder in his hand. What I appreciate of the minister is his serenity; he has not the sombre looks of General McNaughton. I would prefer to have the picture of the minister to one of General McNaughton, because the minister understands that atomic energy is most powerful, but he is not always making depressing speeches, undertaker's speeches, like some that we hear all the time. Life is sad, anybody might die suddenly; it is very sad, but that is the story.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Particularly with the atomic bomb.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: An atomic bomb may explode and kill many people. Until this happens, why should everybody have a sombre look? Every time the atomic bomb is mentioned, why not think of the happy possibilities of the whole thing?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Of being blown to bits.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not serious. I suggest that the matter should be treated seriously, but not in the spirit of an undertaker. Besides that, I will point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that the minister is a qualified engineer. The hon. member for York West is also a qualified engineer. I am not, and the other hon. members who have spoken on it are not engineers. What do they know about the formula of the atomic bomb? They know nothing about it. They have seen pictures in the press and in illustrated periodicals the same as everybody else; they have seen the big cloud of smoke,

Transitional Measures Act
and afterwards they have seen the ravages of destruction. That is all they know about the atomic bomb.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is enough.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
When we see a small part of atomic energy providing the power to move a big ship or a locomotive or an aeroplane or anything of that sort, then we shall have every reason to rejoice. During and before the last war, what did we hear about poison gas? Poison gas was invented before the first war. It was used in the first war. It happened that mustard gas killed some people in some cities of Europe between the two wars, but when the second war started there was an implicit agreement between the belligerent parties not to use poison gas, and it was not used by anybody.
Who knows about the use of atomic energy during a future wair? In the first place, shall we have a future war? Why should we always have panicky speeches about a future war? We are not sure about it. and even if we have it will atomic energy be used by all the belligerent countries? We are not sure about it. Therefore we should have a better philosophy of life and, considering the power of atomic energy and realizing it, we should not always be afraid of it, because it may be a benefit to mankind, most people are hoping. Consequently, why should we worry unduly and make depressing and panicky speeches about the atomic bomb?
I have something else to say. I find it very pleasant that the present Minister of Trade and Commerce is the member of the cabinet who has atomic energy under his jurisdiction to a large extent. He knows a lot about it; he has contributed more than anybody else to the development of that energy, and I am sure that his earnest wish is that it may be used for the benefit of mankind at the earliest possible opportunity.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
All of us recognize that the second report; of the united nations commission on atomic energy does not envisage control of radioactive ores by any international authority, but I cannot accept the government's view that it is a wise policy to permit the mining of uranium-bearing ores by mining interests which have no other interest in the matter than that of making fortunes for a few people.
I am not interested in profits for a few shareholders of such companies that may be interested in the production of these ores, but I am concerned about the potential economic value of such mineral-producing concentrates to the general public. The Minister of Trade
and Commerce will say that the government still have control of uranium because they are the sole purchasing agents. I am sure the minister is quite satisfied that the purchase of concentrates by the government will give the federal authorities far from complete control over such mining development. This sort of control would not eliminate such possibilities as smuggling to other countries where higher prices might be paid than those offered in Canada.
Uranium can be of great economic value in the production of energy. I think that has been indicated in this house by men who should have some reasonable knowledge of that particular subject. It seems to me that if profits are to be made out of a rare mineral of this kind the people of Canada should be the beneficiaries from this great natural resource and it should be the heritage of all Canadians and not of just a few. I saw today a news item in a reputable paper, the Christian Science Monitor, from which I wish to quote some words spoken by so outstanding a physicist, Doctor Lyle B. Borst. This gentleman, I may say, was in charge of developing the Hanford plutonium plant in Washington during the war and is now directing the building of a nuclear reactor at Brookhaven national laboratory in Upton, Long Island, New York. He said;
The industrial applications of atomic energy will be legion but will certainly not be immediate. There are too many problems to be solved in the meantime. But development of atomic power is one of. the most direct and foreseeable future industries.
He says there are certain definite applications such as mobile power for ships, submarines and planes and probably a practical application of atomic power in many other fields. I suggest that in the development of atomic energy for power purposes there are unlimited possibilities. It may take five years, ten years or even a generation, but there seems to be little doubt that the energy from this source will be used in Canada some day, and certainly it will be used elsewhere. Because of this definite trend, which is, we know in its scientific value quite important, I feel that the government should control every avenue of its development. While a minimum price has been set for ores and concentrates, there does not appear to be any indication that a maximum has been placed on the price which may be paid.
This country has had some experience in Ihe past in the alienation of natural resources to private interests, and it has not always made for better living standards among our people. Electrical energy has been one of these
Transitional Measures Act

resources which have been exploited. It has been developed in many cases by private interests and later purchased by municipal or state bodies in order to protect the people from exploitation.
Private interests may develop uranium deposits along similar lines, but what guarantee is there that a monopoly may not shut out the small producer and then hold up the state when these ores are needed for vital economic development?
There the minister makes a reference to very special circumstances in which consideration might be given to the payment of a higher price by the government. I wonder what these very special circumstances would be. Would that possibly envisage the probability of war? We hope that will never occur, but if a war did occur we know that the atomic bomb would certainly come in for definite use. And1 if a war comes, it does not seem to me a very safe prospect to hand over the production of uranium, which is so important in the production of atomic energy, to private enterprise.
I think we should seriously object now, as we certainly should during a wrar period, to the paying of higher prices for an essential ore just to make it possible for shareholders to make profits when the nation is, in all probability, fighting for its life.
No one has any right to profit from war. We had an experience in the last war when profiteers were oblivious of everything else. Apart from war, however, which we all hope will1 never come, our quarrel with this situation should be definitely on the basis of the great economic value of this mineral, and because of that I feel that it should remain in the hands of the people. I therefore strenuously oppose the revocation of these orders, making it possible for private enterprise to get control of so important a commodity.

We all know that the fission of uranium does release a tremendous amount of energy. Ways and means of using that energy are being studied: at the moment, but it is too early to say positively what its economic uses may be. In the United Kingdom it has been announced in the House of Commons that plans are under way to utilize the heat transferred from fission as a means of heating, but here we are not far enough advanced to make an announcement of the kind.
fMr. McKay.]

I would not say. I do not
know what progress they have made. They have made an announcement, and I would not be prepared to say that atomic energy would compete with either coal or electrical power from an economic point of view. The economics of the United Kingdom are somewhat different from those of Canada in that regard.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am definitely in agreement with other speakers of our group. I have opposed the rather casual way in which the Minister of Trade and Commerce treats the subject. I am getting used to the casualness with which he can dispose of economic empires in this country, doing it with a simple shrug of the shoulders or a wave of the hand. I happened to be sitting in this chamber about two and a half years ago, in August, 1945, when the Prime Minister of Canada made a statement during the meeting of provincial premiers, which startled, I am sure, all those within the soundi of his voice. He made a pronouncement, which was startling to all the world, with respect to the first destructive action upon humanity that had been recorded so far as the material about which we are now speaking is concerned'.
For that reason, or at least because of the impressions left with me and the feeling that we have not had a sufficiently broad1 statement from the minister as regards the military protection we are to have in connection with letting everyone who will, or who can afford to do so, dabble in this material under the limited protection the government is giving us, the people of Canada, I must protest against what looks to me like the selling of another important military commodity. I am not concerned at the moment about the details of economic development. I know nothing about, it, and I know nothing about any phase of this work except that we are again selling or allowing to be given away something which belongs to the people of Canada. Yesterday a motion was moved to adjourn the House of Commons to discuss what was a matter of great import to all the Canadian people. Today with a shrug of the shoulders we are to give away something that would protect us.
I wish to ask a concrete question of the minister. I want to know just how much money has thus far been spent by the government of Canada for the purchase of property, equities in properties, mines or anything that is connected with uranium oxide or other radioactive materials that were purchased by the government before, during, or since the

war. Then I want to know how much has been spent by the government for development since the acquisition of these properties. Then, what additional has been spent by way of assisting prospectors to find the materials? I might say that I am not opposed to an individual or a group of small individuals prospecting and finding materials for sale to the government, as was mentioned by the minister. But I certainly fear the cartel or larger corporation which, by stock manipulation and otherwise, will squeeze out the small man who finds the materials which have the value that these radioactive substances appear to have. I fear that then somebody in a swivel-chair will dictate policies to the Canadian people with respect to price and everything else. Would the minister give us some idea of how much Canadian money has been thrown around in this manner?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I wish to conclude, Mr. Speaker, what I was saying the other night about this bill. It seems to be a socialist measure, and there are no half-ways with respect to free enterprise and socialism. A measure cannot be half socialist and half free enterprise. It must be either socialist or free enterprise, and this is why I again urge the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to consider the desire of the farmers of Canada not to have oats and barley under the wheat board but to leave them to be dealt with by free enterprise.
The suggestion has been made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that these grains be handled by the wheat board. Some people are impressed by the word "co-operative". In a committee of this house we have seen what was done by a co-operative in the west; but I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that in my constituency there are co-operatives of farmers who buy their grain from private dealers instead of from the Cooperative Federee, and the price they pay is five or ten cents less than they would have to pay the co-operative. Whether that is because the co-operative is not well administered, or what is wrong, I am not in a position to say; but if one compares the prices of the private merchants with those of the co-operative it will be seen that the prices of the private grain dealers are lower. This is why some co-operatives in my constituency are dealing with private merchants instead of with the Cooperative Federee.

co-operative of which the hon. gentleman speaks pay dividends?

with them about the matter last year. I am not at all opposed to co-operatives. It is all right for the farmers to join together. But fanners are intelligent; they know where to buy, and very often they buy from local merchants instead of from an organization like that. This is my experience; this is what I learn from the farmers of my constituency.
In conclusion, once more I wish to tell my hon. friends of the Social Credit group that I do not want to offend anyone. 'I do not believe in their doctrine, but I know they are very good members of the house and they have the right to their views just as everyone here has a right to his views. In this matter I believe we should be sufficiently open-minded to consider what is best for the people concerned. I have tried to be the interpreter of the feelings of most of the farmers of my constituency in this respect. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of this house that if they consider the matter objectively they will realize that free enterprise has been the salvation of the farmer as well as of all other individuals. It is the best system. So I make a last appeal to those who sponsor this bill, and ask them not to bring coarse grains under the wheat board.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.

Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose I shall take even until six o'clock, even though only fifteen minutes remain. I only wish to record my position with respect to this measure. As I see it, three principles are involved in this bill. The first is the establishment of a pension plan for those concerned with the operation of the wheat board. With respect to that, I think probably it will be unanimously accepted, and certainly I am in favour of it. The second principle dealt with by this legislation involves an increase in the payments to farmers for deliveries of wheat. Again I should think this would be accepted unanimously, and certainly I am in favour of this principle as it is expressed in the bill.
The third feature, however, with which I cannot agree, makes it possible to institute a state monopoly in nearly all grains produced in Canada. In that regard I wish to say only that I am opposed to this socialist principle. I do not follow the hon. member for Temis-eouata (Mr. Pouliot) in most of his statements, but I agree with his opposition to the introduction of this state monopoly. I realize, of course, that this bill does not actually institute a monopoly. It does make that possible, however; and because I know that if it were introducing a monopoly I would have to oppose it. I believe I should declare myself now as holding this view.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
I do not know that such an expression of opinion makes very much difference, but it seems to me that I owe it to myself and to my constituents to make this statement. I was not elected here to bring about the institution of socialism. On the contrary, I was elected in opposition to such an idea; and until my electorate decides to have another sort of representation, or that it wants socialism, I feel that, in order to be true to the people who elected me, I have to oppose any measure which carries out the principle of state monopoly.
When it comes to voting I feel in a sort of quandary, and I imagine all hon. members who have similar views will feel as I do. I am strongly in favour of the provision for an additional payment to the farmer. I am also in favour of the pension provisions contained in the bill. I am in opposition to the third principle, as I have indicated. I believe that probably the bill should be supported and sent to committee, and that is the way I expect to vote. I do so on the understanding that in committee the bill will be divided into two parts and will come back to the house in two pieces, so that the provisions with respect to pensions and increased payments may be dealt with on the one hand, and the matter of state control considered by itself on the other.
I have spoken in this way only because I feel it is a person's duty to make his views known at some time. I have kept my remarks as brief as possible, because I believe it is a duty to the house to allow hon. members to get on with this legislation which, clearly, has majority support in the house.
While I have kept my word in saying that I did not think I would speak until six o'clock -and I observe I have not-I believe I have placed before the house briefly my views on the subject, and I thank hon. members for listening. With that I conclude.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the measure is passed or voted upon, I wish to take a few minutes of the time of the house to summarize our position with respect to the various features of this bill.
The measure before us is one to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act. This bill has four distinctly different features. Some of these we support. One we could support, with one variation in it; and the fourth we find ourselves unable to support.
The first feature of the bill is that which provides a pension fund for the officers and employees of the board. The second gives power to the board to pay to wheat farmers a part of their own money which the government has been holding back from them. The third feature of the bill gives the wheat board the same powers to handle wheat products that it now has in respect of wheat. I presume those wheat products include flour, bran, shorts and the like.
The fourth feature of the bill is one which would force farmers who grow oats and barley to sell those crops only through the wheat board, and thus to accept prices fixed by a government-appointed board, and administered by the same government-appointed board.
With respect to the second and third of these features, as I said a minute ago, we are in agreement. In the matter of pensions to officers and employees I may say that we agree in principle, but we differ as to the manner of assessment of costs for the half of that scheme not borne by the employees. Then, with respect to the fourth feature, namely the one which compels farmers to market through one board, and denies them the right to sell in any other way, we are opposed. We are opposed because, as I said, it forces them to sell to only one board. We are opposed because, in our judgment, by our forcing them to sell in that way they will be forced to accept a price lower than they might otherwise receive.
I wish to discuss each of these four features as briefly as I can. As to the general question of the desirability of pensions for public servants, I believe there is general agreement as to principle. But as to who should pay a part of the cost of that service, there is a good deal of difference of opinion as to where the assessment should be placed. The question before us is not one as to whether it is desirable that the employees of a public institution such as this should qualify for pension. Rather, the pertinent question is this: Who is to pay the cost of those pensions? These are costs which may run into scores, perhaps hundreds of thousands of dollars in the years ahead.
The bill proposes that half the cost of the pension scheme shall be borne by the officers and employees themselves. With respect to that feature, I imagine that there will be substantially unanimous support, as there will be to the general question of providing pensions. If other public or semi-public bodies such as this are to have pensions provided to their employees, there is no reason why this one should not. The question is: Who should be assessed with that part of the cost which is not borne by the employees themselves? That question raises a basic point, namely, as to whether this is a farmers' board charged with responsibility and accepting the responsibility for marketing the farmers' wheat to
Canadian Wheat Board Act

the best advantage, or whether it is a government board charged with the responsibility of being used for something other than that purpose.
If this is a fanners' board charged primarily with the marketing of farmers' crops, farmers' wheat, to the best advantage, then this half of the cost should be assessed against those doing business with the board, namely the farmers of Canada.
Your Honour, I see it is six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to prolong this debate, because I am just as anxious as anyone else in the house to see these cheques go out to the farmers, and therefore I shall be brief.
Let me say at the outset that I do not see why these cheques cannot go out before the bill is passed. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) can impose taxes and make arrangements for collecting them before a bill for that purpose is passed, so that in an emergency like this, when the farmers are waiting anxiously for this money, I do not see why the cheques could1 not be sent out now and the bill be passed later.

Canadian Wheat Board Act
The second part of the bill has to do with pensions for the employees of the wheat board. I have sat in my seat and listened to criticism of that proposal by different members. But the wheat board is really the farmer in business; I personally have always been in favour of a man having some security for his old age, and I do not see how the farmers can take any exception to pensions being provided for the employees of the board. If we employ people to do our business it is only right that we should pay them and treat them fairly. But I should not like to see the minister have the whole say in this matter. I should like to see half a dozen farmers on the advisory committee of the wheat board have some say as to pensions, in order that the interests of the farmer may be safeguarded and the pensions paid in a fair way. The Canadian National Railways has its pension fund and the Canadian wheat board is, in many ways, a similar institution, so that I do not think we can take any exception to providing pensions for the employees of the wheat board.
The third part of the bill, which would bring in barley or oats, is the most contentious part of the bill. Many members object to it and some members are in favour of it. Personally, not only am I in favour of it but I do not think it goes far enough. I cannot understand some of the objections that have been made against the wheat board. My good friend the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), who is not in his place at the moment, has condemned the wrheat board over the distribution of feeds, something with which the wheat board has absolutely nothing to do. 1 have been the guest of the hon. member for Temiscouata before and have an invitation to go back again, and I intend to go back and try, by reasoned argument, to show him how the wheat board will be an advantage not only to the west but to the east as well.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Maybank) were clear-cut in what they had to say. They have no use for the wheat board. They prefer a speculative system.
My good friends the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Miller) did not commit themselves. I have read over their speeches and I see that they want whatever method will give to the farmer the greatest advantage. I think that sums up their position fairly, but really I cannot understand two hon. members who have been raised on the prairies not being able to make up their minds as to which method will be best
for the farmer. I gave them credit for more intelligence and for being able to come to a decision as to w'hich method would be best for the farmer.
Most hon. gentlemen who have spoken against the wheat board have been lawyers. They have pointed out how the farmer will lose his independence if we adopt the wheat board. I cannot understand how a lawyer should1 take that position, because lawyers belong to the strongest union in the world. They are dictated to by the bar association. They are told what they shall do and what they shall not do. When it comes to the farmer organizing for himself and trying to do something better than he has ever done before, what happens? It is said that you are taking away the farmer's independence. That argument will not hold water. The farmer has organized to protect himself. He is doing only what other people have done, and why it should be wrong in his case I cannot understand. If the farmers vote by a majority that they want to market their grain in that way, then it should be logical for them to do it in that way. When it is pointed out that by having a wheat board, we are taking away liberty of the farmer, I can only point out what the lawyers' union would do. If a lawyer breaks any of the rules of the bar association they will unfrock or ungown him; I do not know what they call it. They will deprive him of his living. But no farm organization has ever tried to deprive anybody of his living. The farm, organizations have tried to raise the standard of living of the farmer, and we should not endeavour to throw cold water on the wheat board. The wheat board is not everything I should like to see, but it is something better than we had before, and I hope we shall have more of it in the future.
The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) talked about the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. He can correct me if I am wrong, but I think he said forty per cent of the farmers belonged1 to it. I want to assure the hon. member that the last survey showed that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture have over fifty-five per cent of the farmers of Canada on their books.

speechtext: On a point of privilege, I have been accused of being a lawyer many times, and I have resented and repudiated it. I am not a lawyer.

speechtext: On a point of privilege, I want it known that there are lawyers, members of bar associations, and then there are barber shop and barrack-room lawyers here to whom we are listening all the time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
I did not think I was insulting my hon. friend tonight. I have always respected the lawyers. I may get into difficulties some day and may need to use a lawyer. Therefore I do not want to be too hard1 on them.
It has been said that professional men get to the top of these farm organizations as leaders. I want to correct that misapprehension. I am one of the men who have climbed to the top of the Manitoba federation. I did not do that in one year. I started in the local organization and went to the district organization, then to the provincial and right up to the top. You do not do that unless you have the confidence of the people whom you represent. To say that they are just figureheads or professional leaders is not true. I do not want hon. gentlemen to believe that, because it is not true. You have to climb that ladder and have the support of the farmers who send you there before you can go that distance.
I regret that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has not seen fit to include rye in this bill; it should have been included. Speculators in rye raised the price to $4.05 a bushel. Until last year the miller paid 64J cents a bushel for his rye, and the speculator was paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Somebody may say to me, "Well, the farmer got his share of that". I am going to ask, what percentage did he get? He did not get the percentage that the speculators got. As most hon. members know, I am against the speculators market. I do not think it is the right and

proper way for the farmers to sell grain. It might have been all right in 1903 but not today.
Three groups are interested in the speculative market. There are the farmers, the millers and the grain handling firms. You must have the speculators to buy hedges. The speculative market cannot operate unless you have the speculator to come in. Have hon. members considered who the speculator is? A survey was made on the Chicago board of trade of the people who were carrying on speculation to keep the farmers' price going up and down, to take up the hedges. "When the government looked to see who was trading in wheat on the Chicago board of trade one day last fall they found, amongst the 3,287 speculators, six clergymen, twenty-four students, six butlers and maids, 308 housewives, 846 farmers, 181 barbers, butchers and bakers and even 44 unemployed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: No lawyers?

speechtext:
The minister does not want me to tell him about the lawyers; I shall let them go this time. I know a great many commissions have sat in my province-I think there have been about eighteen altogether- to look into the marketing of grain and inquire into the futures market. All of them have either approved or condoned the futures market or the futures trade. The fact that so many inquiries have been held in such a short space of time is definite proof that the speculative grain market has failed to give the farmers satisfaction. Can hon. members imagine what would happen if other people had to depend on speculation in a market like that for their bread and butter?
May I quote what I heard another man say, and I have tried to copy it as correctly as I could. Speaking of the results that would follow if everybody were in a speculative market, not only the farmer but everybody else, he states that the effect would be something like this:
Let us suppose that other classes of people in Manitoba obtained their financial rewards under a speculative system. The results would perhaps be something like this:	We would read in
the morning's paper that with few exceptions, the market is weak all along the line today. May carpenters were quoted steady to 25 cents off. The market for July plumbers lacked serious support and reacted to a persistent try by short sellers by dropping 30 cents below yesterday's average. Or we might read that weakness was most pronounced in the barber's pit, -where the price of December haircuts dropped 30 cents, while plain shaves for December delivery decreased five points to 15J cents. Or we might read that the only strong point in

Excise Tax Act Amendment
the labour market was in stenographers, where a squeeze put the price up to $25 a week. Or let us suppose that our Manitoba farmers were to read in the morning paper that May tractors showed a decline of $75 from yesterday's final quotations, or that January refrigerators dropped $40, or spot seed drills were steady at $8 below yesterday's closing. Or it may be that we would read that an unusually large crop of doctors graduated from Canadian universities, and as a result the cost of appendix operations dropped $10 in the medical exchange this morning.
All this may be considered amusing, but such are the conditions under which the fanner is expected to market his produce by those who champion the speculative system in normal times. Many farmers believe what the late President Roosevelt said:
Over-production, under-production and speculation are three evil sisters. Over-production and under-production are about as good for speculators as overindulgence or undernourishment is to the medical profession.
I had the pleasure of being at Lake Success when that great little fighter, the late Mayor LaGuardia, spoke at the food conference. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) was there and so was the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), when that gentleman spoke and condemned speculation. And, by the way, I may say that when I was at the united nations I paid my own expenses. I do not want anyone to get the idea that somebody else paid them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext: You deserve credit for that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EMPLOYEES' PENSIONS, MINIMUM PRICE OF WHEAT DELIVERIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Here is what the late Mayor LaGuardia said:
"You cannot have both stability in prices and security for the farmer els well as fluctuation in prices. It is no use saying that we are not going to interfere with free exchange and free sales. If you want what is needed," Mr. LaGuardia warned, "you will interfere, and you will put every gambling grain exchange out of business in Chicago, Winnipeg, in Liverpool or wherever it exists."
There were fifty-four nations represented around that table that morning. Nobody spoke against that statement, and Canada was represented there. If we disagreed with that statement, our representatives should have stood up and condemned it and declared that we wanted a speculative market. No one advocates that any other producer of goods should sell his produce on a speculative market, because he would be at the mercy of the speculator. I am sure no one would expect the Cockshutt Plow Company, Massey-Harris, or any of the other manufacturers to sell their goods on a speculative market, and I do not think the farmer should be expected to do so.
While there has been rumblings in the west and grumbling about the price paid for wheat, and dissatisfaction in more ways than one, the idea of a central agency to handle grain has had the approval of most of the western farmers. I think that has been pretty definitely agreed to, that the farmer in the west wants orderly marketing through a grain board or a cereal board, call it what you like. But if we are ever to build up that ever-normal granary to provide for drought years or grasshopper years, we must get away from speculative marketing and get down to orderly marketing through a wheat board or some organization similar to that.
On motion of Mr. Mcllraith the debate was adjourned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

When we last had this resolution before us I had pointed out to the minister that in his opening speech he had said that the main purpose of the new taxes is to save United States dollar exchange. Other reasons were given, but I suggested to the minister that we should not be asked to vote on this resolution until we had some estimate-and after all, some months have elapsed now since it came into effect- of the amount of United States exchange which is, in fact, being saved. I suggested, as best I could, a certain method which the minister might follow, and I am bound to say he did not think much of it. I also suggested to him that no doubt his officials would have a better method of doing it, and I hope that tonight he will be able to give us some figures. I might remind the minister that there were three or four reasons given for the passage of the bill, to be founded on the resolution, but this was the first and most important, and I suggest that some figures should now be given the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Following the discussion we had some days ago when this matter was before the committee, I discussed it again with the officials. I am sure one cannot give in dollars

and cents the saving of United States exchange which might result from the imposition of deterring taxes of this kind. Of course the initial saving in articles that are subject to the tax will come as a result of the operation of schedule III of the import restriction bill. There will be an incidental saving, and an incidental saving only if the tax will then slow down the consumption of the articles which are being manufactured in Canada and which are already subject to some control, shall we say, by the operation of schedule III.
I do not suppose one can yet say that there is any backing up of sales of, let us say, automobiles. In the case of automobiles, schedule III, through the foreign exchange control board order in council, has been in operation for a matter of only two or three weeks. Therefore I again say that I do not see how, at this stage, I could possibly be expected to express in terms of dollars and cents what the saving would be. There is the second effect, as my hon. friend appreciates, which is desired, and that is the general slowing down of consumption in Canada in order to create again this over-all current account surplus of which I have spoken. I have asked my officials if they can give even a rough estimate of what effect this might have had expressed in terms of dollars and cents, and they tell me it is impossible to do so. I may have misunderstood what my hon. friend wanted. If I have, perhaps he will try to show me where I have misunderstood him.

I will try. In the first place, I have a feeling as this goes on, that however much we may have disliked certain features of Bill No. 3, the embargo, nevertheless it has teeth in it and it can act. In connection with that we obtained, although with some difficulty, figures from the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to what the government thought it might achieve in the way of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister said what it would do in the future.

Yes. I appreciate that this is different. But nevertheless I still suggest that these figures could be obtained. First of all, I am surprised if this is being brought forward with no estimated figures of any kind. I wonder if the minister really wants to go so far as to state that. In the second place, I suggest that, while the embargo has been in effect for only a few weeks, this tax has already been in effect for a few months-actually since November last. Surely the saving which will be effected by this is, in effect, the saving by reason of the

Excise Tax Act Amendment
slowing up, as the minister said a moment ago, of the manufacture of Canadian goods into which United States parts go. Are we in agreement on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is accurate. I would hope that the imposition of this fairly stiff tax of 25 per cent on a line of semi-luxury articles, shall we call them, would have the effect of getting people to slow down in their purchases. That is the intention. If this objective is not achieved, the tax will of course, have failed. But it will at least have this effect, that if people spend their money on these things, they will not have it to spend on something else and force the prices of those things up.
The minister is now bringing in what I call his deflationary argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is all right.

I think we want to stick to one thing at a time and that, when we are trying to assess one reason, we should not go off to another. I am not underestimating the difficulties, but I am saying and repeating, perhaps a little tiresomely, that I do not think we should be asked to go it blind in this thing. There should be some estimate. We happen to be in the position that the thing has already been in operation for three months. I now come back to my suggestion. My suggestion is that it is perfectly feasible to find the sales which were taking place in the classes of goods before November 17 and the sales which were taking place after that date, when the tax came into effect. I am not suggesting [DOT] that is a perfect test. I know there are certain qualifications in that which the minister will want to make and which I might make for him. But I still suggest that these figures would give us some prima facie evidence as to whether or not any definite effect is being produced. Suppose it is found actually that the consumption of these things in Canada has been greater since November. The minister might say he expects to find them greater because of the cutting off of United States goods. I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say-
May I finish?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I suggest that this is a figure which could be obtained. I cannot think there is any difficulty in getting that because, after all, I understand the department from month to month, through its agents, visits the various companies and examines the taxation records; therefore they know the consumption., production and sale of the articles in question. The producers can equally well give the figures before November 17. Therefore I do not think the figure is an impossible one to get.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It may not be absolutely impossible. I cannot say that it is. But the officials tell me that they cannot obtain or cannot yet give an accurate estimate of what the result is. On the question of cars and radios may I say this. I have had numerous discussions with representative groups of car manufacturers and radio manufacturers, because they are two of the larger groups. The car manufacturers do not claim that the tax has yet slowed down the consumption of cars. They tell me that they think it will. Whether they are right or wrong, I do not know. The same thing applies to the radio people. No one has contended to me that the sale of radios has yet been diminished. But the radio manufacturers who come in tell me that they are most apprehensive as to what the result will be in the near future. I tell them that I hate to say it but I am glad to hear that, because that is the sort of thing I am trying to accomplish with this tax. I wish I could give my hon. friend the figures. I think he will bear me out when I say that I am the last man who ever tries to keep figures from this house. If the information is available, I want to give it. But I have not been able to get from the officials, or they are not prepared to give me, an estimate which they believe can give any accurate indication of what the effect of this new tax has been on sales. I put on Hansard a week or so ago the total tax collections on this group, and I gave the estimated increased tax. Those are the only figures that the officials tell me they can give. To try to pull out of that what the sales would have been had the tax not been on, is something which the national revenue department tell me they cannot do.

I suggest that the minister has really not said that these figures cannot be obtained. Rather what he has said is that he does not think the thing has gone on long enough yet to achieve the hoped-for result. He says he hopes that will come later. That is a perfectly legitimate hope. I say again that I realize the difficulty of the question I am asking; nevertheless I do not believe that it is impossible for these figures to be obtained.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

I still suggest that these figures should be obtained so that we are not asked to vote on something absolutely blind, as we are now being asked to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am a little bit lost in this. I really would like to give my hon. friend the information for which he asks. Perhaps the officials could go into the figures and estimate what tax would have been collected had there been no increase and try to translate that into the number of units, and that could be applied to radios and automobiles. But this tax covers a much wider field than that. Suppose my hon. friend had that information. I do not wish to be offensive, but what good would it do him? What conclusion could he draw from it? After two or three months' operation, and with stocks in hand, I do not see what useful information that would give him.
It seems to me that it is reasonable for me to say this: Suppose these figures are obtained and that they show that up to the present there is no sign of any saving in United States exchange at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But we cannot tell whether it has saved United States exchange or not.

I am not so sure. I am not under-estimating the difficulties, and I do not intend to persist in this unduly; but I still do not think the minister has told me that the figures cannot be obtained. What the minister has said is that he thinks that, when the figures are obtained, they will not show anything that will be enlightening. Maybe not. Maybe I shall have to admit that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend this. I think the sales of radios, since this tax went into effect, have been just as great as they were before. I make that assertion. I do not know whether it is true but possibly it is the case. I am sure that the sales of domestically produced automobiles have been just as great. The purchasing power in this country is such, and the demand for automobiles at the moment is such, that people will buy them whether or not there is an extra 25 per cent tax. But one cannot judge the ultimate results of this on the initial one, two or three months' operations, and I do not believe any figures one would give as to tax receipts for the first two or three months would prove anything at all. I could give those figures; I gave them before.

Not exactly the ones I am asking for. It seems to me that what the minister is saying

is not that we cannot have those figures, but that he thinks they will not be any good to us if we get them. Coming back to what I said before, I would say that if the figures on automobiles and radios prove what he suggested a moment ago, namely, that there has been no reduction, I will frankly concede to the minister that this does not necessarily mean the tax is no good; but equally I say it does not prove the tax is good. In other words, surely the minister cannot ask us to vote for something without some further indication than just a kind of reasoning on general principles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, the minister and the government proceed on the assumption that the imposition of a tax will have the effect which is generally accepted among economists and1 those who know something about fiscal methods; that is, that it will slow down consumption of the article which is taxed. Perhaps the wealth and spending power of this country are such that this tax will not have that effect. Perhaps the tax is inadequate; perhaps we should have made it 50 per cent or 75 per cent. I do not think so. I can only be assertive, but I believe the tax will accomplish the results, or will help to accomplish the results we are trying to achieve. If it should not, then, of course, it would have been useless to impose it, but I do not think we can determine that at this stage of the game.

Then let me ask just one other question. I repeat that the reason I am being persistent in this is that I think you have already in your hands one weapon which is effective, and I have very great doubts as to whether this new weapon is effective. Also I have no doubt whatever that it is offensive to a large number of people.
There is another consideration which enters in here, and in this connection there should be a figure which can be obtained. That is, even if this slowing down process does occur, then coming back to our test in connection with United States exchange, all you are saving is the lowered amount of United States parts that go into these articles; that is to say, the lowered amount of United States parts that are used. Some of these things have a trifling amount of United States parts, and some have none at all. That is the other figure for which I asked the other night which, if it were found, I think might show that, as far as the saving of United States exchange is concerned, this measure is trivial.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Surely I do not have to go into my reduction of consumption thesis again

Excise Tax Act Amendment
and point out that if we are to continue to ship goods abroad on credit, somehow or another we must reduce our domestic consumption and create again this over-all current account surplus we have lost. The fiscal method is one way of doing that. My criticism of this tax, if I were speaking from the point of view of economics and were sitting across the way, would be that it does not cover a wide enough field; that it should cover more; that it should not be restricted to electrical equipment, cars and so on, but that we should go into a wider field. That might be a valid criticism; but when my hon. friend says it will not accomplish the results expected he is being assertive, and I can only be assertive and say I hope it will.
The minister is now changing to another argument. It may be a good argument, but I want to bring him back-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know what I said in my opening remarks, but I am not tied to that as the only reason for which this tax is being imposed.
No, you are not tied to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No one will contend that.

No. I have said there are several other reasons, but I think it proper to say the minister pointed out that this was the main reason. If the main reason turns out to be valid, then we are entitled to doubt the other reasons as well. I want to see what validity there is in this main reason, first of all. It may turn out that it is not the main reason at all; that there are other, better reasons; but I submit that we are entitled to find out if this main reason is a real reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can answer my hon. friend only by saying I think it is too soon for us to judge. In putting this forward, the government believes it will accomplish these results. The initial results of the over-all program have been good. Perhaps six months from now we shall be in a better position to see whether it is really doing what we hope it will. I wish I could give my hon. friend the figures he would like to have, but I do not seem able to do so. I cannot help that.

I will ask the minister perhaps a little easier question, if the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has finished. If we are able to cut the consumption of these things at home, I understand from the minister that we shall send the surplus to the United States, if possible, to try and get United States dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily.
I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that. But my understanding is that the United States customs authorities intend to take this 25 per cent into account when they put on their tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We dealt with that the other evening; but we are not shipping cars back to the United States.
It is not just cars I am thinking about. I have in mind refrigerators and all the other things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we cut down the consumption of refrigerators and other articles which contain metal, we can sell the metal in its original form for dollars in the United States or anywhere else. That is one way whereby we can get United States exchange. Instead of using labour in Canada to convert the metal into things our own people consume, we shall sell the raw materials. We can sell all the copper, all the nickel, all the aluminum and so on, we produce; and we can sell it for hard currency.
Does the minister say none of the things in this schedule are being exported to the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have pretty well taken out of the schedule those articles in which we have an export market in the United States. As I explained on earlier occasions, that was one reason we took out such things as hot plates, because some of our manufacturers have built up a market for those articles in the United States. The same is true of golf clubs. One may ask why we would take golf clubs out of the list. We found that some of our manufacturers had developed a profitable export market in the United States. The same thing applies to golf balls. That is why we took these sporting goods out of the schedule, because there were these export opportunities in the United States. But we do not and cannot export refrigerators to the United States; at least we never have done so. We have never exported cars to the United States. I do not know about radios.
Did the minister make representations to the United States authorities?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. If my hon. friend will look at page 2131 of Hansard he will see the explanation I gave the other evening in reply to the hon. member for Kindersley. We made
Excise Tax Act Amendment

representations. Under the Geneva agreements the United States have undertaken to change their practice so that a tax of this kind would not be included for duty purposes. But that requires legislative action by congress, and until the legislative action has been taken, the United States customs authorities are obliged to include the tax. My hon. friend will find that information in Hansard as I have indicated; an hon. member from Toronto asked me the same question.

The farther we go, the more confusing this becomes. I have listened to the explanations given by the minister, and he has not yet put us in possession of any facts or figures to prove that this is right. In other words, it would appear that so far it has been a bit of guesswork, much the same as the last two budgets which have been presented to this house. Each made a forecast which was out by millions upon millions of dollars. It seems to me that, irrespective of what the minister says, the object of this is to raise more revenue; in any event that seems to be one of the results.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We took off some taxes at the same time.

Let me say this, and I say it with great respect for the minister because he did give an explanation. I remind you, Mr. Chairman, that there are two schools of thought. One school believes this could have been done by leaving our dollar devalued and having the 90-cent dollar or the 81-eent dollar, or whatever it might be. The minister has explained that; and I suppose the same people are advising him now who advised him then.
Another explanation the *minister gave was that, because of the trend toward inflation in the United States, he felt it was necessary to bring our dollar on a par with the United States dollar. May I ask this: Can the minister tell me why he would place our dollar on a par with the United States dollar, where it would buy a dollar's worth of United States goods and by the same token on November 17 reverse the position and say that the Canadian dollar was worth only seventy-five cents?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would love to debate this question of devaluation with the hon. member for Grey North, and I have already made several statements on it. However it is not strictly relevant to the committee's discussion of this ways and means resolution, and I think I must reserve that discussion to some other time.

All I am trying to get at is this. You have now devalued the Canadian dollar in the home market by the imposition of this excise tax. You are saying, "For numerous goods your dollar will buy only seventy-five cents worth; and the other twenty-five cents goes to the government."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friend. We are exercising selective devaluation, not across-the-board devaluation.

Selective devaluation is resting in the hands of a group of bureaucrats. We have very little to say about directing their course. That same group are advising the minister, and they have got into effect this measure which has already been said to be unconstitutional. And you are going to depend upon the government's majority sitting behind you to pass it.

I should like to ask the minister a plain question, one which is not quite so complicated as some of the others which have been asked. As I have come up to these buildings in the last few days I have seen some small cards in the windows of stores where magazines are sold. These cards read, "Back on Canadian newsstands, True Romances and True Story". How does that help us save United States dollars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it does. I imagine that the enterprising publishers of these delightful publications have arranged to put them out in Canada. I am only guessing, but I think that must be so. They are certainly prohibited, so far as entry into Canada is concerned.
Still prohibited.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They must be printing them here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must remind hon. members that we are dealing with the Excise Tax Act. Magazines do not come into this discussion; they do not come within the act, at all.
I shall not ask the question again.

There is one question I wish to ask the minister. I have heard him say on many occasions that one of the reasons for putting on this excise tax is the fact that we are exporting on credit. I should like to ask him if he is absolutely certain that we are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not put it that way.
It means the same thing. AVe both mean the same thing. I should like

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Excise Tax Act Amendment
to ask him if he is quite satisfied that we are actually exporting on credit. I ask that because I heard the Minister of Agriculture say that these are not really loans, but rather that they are gifts which will never be repaid. Are we exporting on credit or are we actually making gifts of these goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I answered that the other day in reply to a question by the hon. member for Kamloops. I said that these credits are being made under the terms of a contract which calls for repayment. As Minister of Finance, I expect that contract to be carried out. Of course, under existing conditions it would perhaps be unreasonably optimistic to expect all of this loan to be met at maturity. And there will unquestionably or probably be some loss. We set by each year in our accounts out of current revenue the amount of 825,000,000, I believe it is, in a reserve to take care of loss on inactive assets; just as businessmen would do. I cannot give my hon. friend any other answer.
All right. The minister expects at some future day that a large number of these loans will be repaid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would hope so, yes.

So that all we need to do is to ask the people to defer their spending until a future day, or until such time as these nations pay for what they receive. Then these goods will be available for the people to buy. That being so, would it not be satisfactory for the government, as the hon. member for Peace River suggested, to float a loan to buy food for these countries, such loan to be subscribed from the savings of the people? I am not suggesting that the government should borrow from the banks, because that would mean an expansion. But would it not be possible for the government to borrow the savings of the people and in that way reduce the demand for goods, so as to make those goods available for other countries? Then, when those nations repay the loan the government will be able to repay the loan made from the people, and the people will have money with which to buy goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That would be effective only if the floating of such a loan and subscriptions to it by the people resulted in effective reduction in consumption in this country; if the people, as a result of having put their money into these loans, and having no other money to use for the purchase of commodities, would be unable to or would voluntarily refrain from purchasing consumption or capital goods in this country or importing them from the
United States. Otherwise we could float loans until we were blue in the face without helping our balance of payments position.
No one understands better than my hon. friend that the crux of this balance of payments difficulty is this, that we have ceased to have in this country an over-all current account surplus. In other words, we are consuming just about as much as we are producing.
That is not the crux of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The minister has been putting forward to the people, or it was put to them at one time, that it was necessary for them to buy bonds in order to curtail spending. It seems to me that if the government were to carry on the same program, explaining to the people the necessity for helping foreign nations by supplying goods, and by asking the people in the lower income brackets to buy bonds for that purpose, it would not have to float loans with the people in the high-income brackets. Then the minister would agree that it would have the effect he desires, and probably it would do it more effectively than the excise tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is possible. The people bought these bonds during wartime, and rightly so, under wartime conditions. But now the war is over and a great many people naturally want to go out and buy new refrigerators, new radios, new washing machines and all the rest of it. That is a very natural thing to do. But unfortunately we are not yet in a position, because of these world difficulties, to which I have referred, where the people can fully gratify those wishes; that is, if we are to continue to play our part in helping in the recovery of the devastated countries.
Mr. SMITH {Calgary West): I wish to ask one or .two questions. The first one deals with what has just been discussed by the hon. member for Acadia. It is this: Did I understand the Minister of Finance correctly a minute ago when he said, as I thought, that he figured these loans would be paid, although not altogether on their due date. Did I understand him to say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have said twice that they are made under terms which call for repayment, and I expect them to be repaid. It would perhaps be unreasonably optimistic to expect they would all be repaid. That is what I have said. And the portion that would not be repaid would be small. I have no reason
Excise Tax Act Amendment

to think, for instance, that the United Kingdom would not live \jp to its obligations. She has always done so in the past. I expect she will continue to do so.

I am sure she will, if she can. The point I make is this. Apparently the Minister of Finance takes the position directly opposite to that of the Minister of Agriculture, who told us in this chamber within the past three weeks that everybody knew that a great portion of these loans would never be repaid. Apparently those views have to be reconciled one way or another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a matter of opinion.
I turn to the second question; and it is amazing to see me as an economist at the present time. But I do know these simple things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably better than the rest of us.

The minister told us a few minutes ago that it was a well known law of economics that the higher the price, the less purchases were made; with which law I am in entire agreement. I think he will also agree that, having regard to articles in the luxury class of goods, those luxury goods would be purchased largely by people with plenty of money, and that the law would not apply, for example, as it would in respect of food and clothing. It ceases to have the same effect when you go up that stairway. That would, I think, be a correct statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a general statement I think that is all right.

My general statement is just the same as the minister's, so that I think he will agree with me. We cannot get much closer than that. The suggestion I make to the minister is this, that he will at least admit that, in the four months' experience he has had with this excise tax, he sees no evidence that there is a saving from it in United States dollars or that there is not. Is that the position now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To be strictly accurate, we have been saving United States dollars. We have reversed a loss of $70 million by a gain last month of $13 million. How much of that is due to the tax, how much to direct controls, and how much to a number of other factors, I cannot say nor can anyone else, but it appears that the program is doing what it was intended to do. That is all I can say.

That is not what I asked. It is fairly easy, you know, if you take it gently. All I ask the minister to admit is this. Aside from what he has just said, at the present time he has no evidence that this excise tax in these four months has saved United States dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And I never shall have evidence, because this is only one part of a three-pronged program, and I shall never be able to pin the gain on any one facet.
Then, as a part of this austerity program the minister admits that he will never know whether this excise tax has succeeded or not. That is the statement he has just made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have pretty good evidence wThen I see the exchange saving each month.
Maybe you will, but a moment ago you said you would not.

This subject is becoming somewhat technical and I do not feel competent to attack it on that level. I have been wondering what the housewives in the gallery and in the country think about this particular tax. I was thinking of it rather from the point of view of the family man. When the minister said he was well aware that he had not become a national hero through the imposition of this tax, I think he was making an understatement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I never thought it was a popularity gaining move, and I said so.

This new excise tax does not bring much comfort to the already harassed consumer. I do not think I am competent to enter into a discussion of the constitutionality of the tax, although at school I did learn that a principle of British parliamentary procedure was' that there would be no taxation without the consent of the people taxed; and I find it difficult to accept the only defence the minister could give for the imposition of this tax in his announcement over the radio on November 17, that the tax would be effective on the morning of the 18th or thereabouts, was that it was necessary, and that he hoped to get the consent of parliament to the imposition of the tax, which later on he told us is not a tax until it is passed by parliament. In the meantime, as has been pointed out by the various speakers, the tax has been collected, as most heads of families are very well aware. Incidentally the minister has not yet obtained the consent of this house to the tax.

Excise Tax Act Amendment
and I am wondering what would happen in case the house withheld its consent, because I am not one of those who believe that refunds would be made on the basis of purchase slips because many of these purchase slips carry no record of the purchase. So far as I am concerned, I think the government's action was inexcusable, particularly for a government based upon a party which has always loudly proclaimed that taxation is the function of parliament and that the will of parliament is supreme.
There are two matters which I am advancing in the form of questions. I take it that the first main reason for this particular tax is to reduce in this country the purchase of goods we import from abroad or goods made up of parts imported from other countries. Many householders have been waiting for years to purchase these household goods which are now taxed heavily. They were urged during the war to purchase bonds to keep purchasing power out of the hands of the people; and now, when purchasing power comes into their hands and they thought they would have an opportunity to buy that refrigerator, they find they cannot do so because of this tax.
My question is this: If it were necessary to cut down the imports from the United States in order to conserve United States exchange, and it may have been, why would it not have been feasible or practicable for the minister by some method to see to it that Canadian manufacturers would not take advantage of that situation? Could there not have been a ceiling? There have been ceilings before. They were abandoned only a short time ago. Could a ceiling not have been reimposed on this particular type of goods so that people who, in perfect good faith, had co-operated with the government in the purchase of bonds, people in the small income brackets, would have been able to buy these goods which the minute the tax was imposed they found they could not buy because there was a competitive sellers' market in which the people in the low-income brackets could not compete. These goods were not available to people in the low-income brackets once this tax was imposed. That is my first question, whether it would not have been practicable to impose a ceiling on these things, and, if not, why, so that people in the low-income brackets could have obtained some of these goods and not have had to compete with people with more money.
My second question is this. I take it that one of the remedies for this situation would be the tremendously increased production of Canadian goods. I would ask the minister, and the government through him, why it was that a great amount of machinery for the manufacture of goods which had come into the possession of the country was scrapped or sold for a very small percentage of its value when, if the government is genuine in its belief that more goods are necessary in this country, such machinery could have been used for the production of these goods which, for years, the public had wanted and done without.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
First, as to the imposition of ceilings, that would have meant, in the view of the government, the resumption of practically over-all price control and the resumption of rationing, and it was felt that this was not feasible.
As to increasing production by additional machinery, there is no lack of production in Canada today because of a lack of machinery. Every bit of machinery is being utilized. One of the reasons we have lost a good deal of United States dollars has been the heavy imports of machinery from the United States. Not only are all the existing production facilities of the country being utilized but they are being rapidly expanded. I said, when discussing this matter the other evening, that possibly production could be increased in this country by increased efficiency and the working of longer hours and so on, but by and large we are working at nearly full employment now, and I question whether, with the existing manpower, the existing hours of labour and the existing techinques, the productive capacity of this country could be greatly expanded. Many of our essential production processes depend upon the importation of essential materials from the United States. That would have involved still further expenditures of United States dollars.

I believe that, as the questioning goes on and the facts come out in connection with this matter it becomes less desirable. AVe were told definitely at the beginning that this was a measure to conserve that portion of import commodities in those commodities which are taxed and which may come from the United States. That was given as the chief reason by the minister on several occasions. Then, after some persistent questioning from this side of the house, another interesting factor came out, and was disturbing too, namely that the minister told us later another reason was that the government was anxious to preserve the market for United States businessmen who had been selling these commodities in Canada until the time that this matter came up. That was a revealing piece of information and one which-*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It did not come out after questioning. I pointed that out in my radio speech as an essential provision.
Excise Tax Act Amendment
We can be forgiven for not remembering-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not result from any cross-examination by my hon. friend or anyone else.

We can be forgiven for not-remembering what the minister said over the radio, because it is such a long time ago; it is almost history; but it has come out now, and I am sure that the Canadian people-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take objection to the "now." It was announced at the same time that the program was announced.
That is fine. I am sure that the Canadian businessman engaged in the selling of these commodities or the manufacturer who is engaged in manufacturing them will not thank the minister for that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are not asking for protection, are you?

No; you are giving the United States businessmen protection. If anyone is to get protection, then certainly our citizens are the first ones entitled to it.
Another thing that has come out-I will not say "now," because apparently the minister does not like that expression-through the questions which have been fired back and forth is that this policy is designed so as to discourage the buying of commodities in Canada, regardless of whether they have any United States import content in them or not. The minister has told us that. I believe it came out. after questioning. What it adds up to is simply this. The government apparently believes that, by taxing the Canadian people 25 per cent on these articles, they will release that amount of purchasing power which would have gone into these articles, for the purpose of purchasing something else. I believe the minister will agree with that, because he has said on several occasions if they do not spend their money on these articles, then they will have that money to spend on something else, which he hopes will be essentials such as the things that go into production and even capital goods and so on. If that is the case, then the government must admit that they made a terrible blunder when they started decontrolling about a year ago.
It will be remembered that the first things that were decontrolled in this country-and all we have to do is look up the records-were what were called luxury goods. In other words, when the time for reconversion was on its way in this country, when there was an opportunity to direct the economy toward the

production of essential commodities, what did the government do? They took price control off these commodities which were non-essential; they took controls off luxury commodities-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We are not now dealing with decontrol.

I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this is pertinent, because what the minister is attempting to do by placing this tax on these commodities is to discourage the consumption of what he calls semi-luxury goods. If you discourage the consumption of these goods it also means you discourage the proproduction of them, because there would be no object in producing them if nobody will buy them.
