I imagine that the government was-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. We have had quite a lengthy debate on these controls.

Mr. Chairman, you will note that I am not debating the merits of price control as such. At the moment I am only pointing out that, had the government used the power of price control which they still had in their hands-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would not have to do this.

-at the present time, then they would not have to use this excise tax to the same extent that they are now using it. I believe that is a sound argument. What is more, they would have protected the consumer in the lower income brackets to a greater extent than is now done. What has happened now is that, by decontrolling first of all the so-called luxury articles in this country, the government gave an impetus to the production of these non-essentials. Then, having found that there were too many of them on the market and people spending their money on so-called semi-luxury doodads the government says, "We will not only stop you from buying luxury goods, but we will stop you from buying semi-luxury goods as well by asking you to pay 25 per cent more."
What are some of these so-called semiluxury goods? We could have a debate on what is a necessity and what is not because, when I look down the list, I find, for example, a rather small article, but a very necessary one, particularly so when I look around here, because we are practically all men. I find that shaving brushes are not taxed, but razors and shavers are. There will be some pretty grizzly looking characters around here in a

Excise Tax Act Amendment
year or so, because no one can shave with a shaving brush, you must have a razor along with it.
That will be the new look for men.
Our beards will be down to our knees.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Shaving brushes are not taxed.

No, but razors and
shavers are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because there was an export market for these goods.
You can lather up your face and go out; you cannot shave.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You can, unless you use an electric razor. My hon. friend1 may use these expensive electric razors. I use the old-fashioned1 Gillette. There are no taxes on those.
You are a real Tory.

Seriously though, there are in this list commodities which cannot be called luxury goods. It cannot be argued that these articles are luxury items for all the people. For example, let us take automobiles. There are thousands of people in this country who depend for their livelihood on owning and driving an automobile. Go into the field of salesmanship. There are a lot of people who work in the civil service, for example, who have travelling jobs; they are people who earn their living by owning and operating a car. Had the minister placed a tax on cars which are priced at from $2,000 upward, it might not have been so bad because then you could say that anyone who makes a living by owning and operating an automobile will not buy a Cadillac or a Buick or any one of these expensive cars; he will be satisfied with a cheaper model. But no, the tax starts from $1,200, which means that there is not an automobile on the market today which you can buy without paying the excise tax. This means that there will be thousands of people across this country who will find it 25 per cent harder to make a living than before.
We find that articles for household use such as refrigerators and all kinds of electrical appliances are taxed so that people who are trying to buy them in the western provinces, where unfortunately our electrification schemes have not gone forward as fast as they have in some other parts of the country on account of the depression we had there, are finding it exceedingly difficult. Today those provinces
are attempting to start rural electrification schemes and they run smack into these taxes. They find that the people for whom they are planning this electrification are beginning to become lukewarm over the matter and are not enthusiastic because the price of the goods they have to buy has gone up 25 per cent. The difficulty of the government is-and I say this sincerely-they are attempting to get the effect or the result of a planned economy without doing any planning. They are attempting to get out of the so-called free enterprise system the same result as they would get out of a planned economy, but they have refused to do that supplementary or complementary part, which is to have a planned economy in the first place; I do not know what this committee can do except to register its protest. If the government were to be fair with this committee they would separate from this list the last two parts of the resolution, paragraphs 5 and 6, which have to do with the taking off of the tax. That part could be taken separately, in a separate bill if necessary, and the committee could decide on the merits of this tax alone. I do not think it is wise to attempt to confuse the public and parliament by proposing in the same debate to tax the people 25 per cent or more, at the same time pointing to another part of the resolution ajid saying, "Oh, we are taking the tax off electricity and sugar". If we are to 'have a taxation scheme let us make our decision and deal with that by itself and deal with the other aspect separately. If it were put in that way, and if private members opposite were given a free vote, I am confident that the resolution would not carry.

It seems to me that we talk in millions so often in this house that it is difficult to get a genuine appreciation of just how this affects the ordinary citizen. During the war we had compulsory savings and there was the sale of something which was popular, namely war savings certificates for $4. This year that little savings certificate will be due and will be worth $5. I wonder if it has occurred to the Minister of Finance, when he thinks about this, that people who have been saving in this way over a period of years would like now to buy some of the luxuries and even the necessities for which they have been waiting so long a time to acquire-a refrigerator, an automobile or something else that might appeal to them. Has it occurred to the minister that his 25 per cent excise tax will take every cent that the little war savings certificate earned? People have invested their money in war savings certificates in the last seven and a half years, and now they will find
Excise Tax Act Amendment

that the dollar they have earned on every four dollars they invested will be taken from them when they attempt to spend their money for something which is necessary in their homes.
In view of the minister's statement that the purpose of the tax is to restrict consumption, how long does he expect it will be necessary to enforce this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot make any forecast as to the length of time it will last. That will depend upon how our balance of payments position works out. The reserves today, while improving, are far below what they should be and far below what I should like them to be. I cannot say how long it will be necessary to continue these restrictive measures; but, as I have said on numerous occasions, I do not wish to keep them on a day or an hour longer than is necessary.

May I ask the minister this question? If the Marshall plan in the
United States goes through in the next few weeks, can he give any undertaking that the taxes will be taken off?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give any undertaking. Of course that is an important factor, as it is bound to be, in helping to restore our balance of payments position.

I wish to ask a question which I think will simplify matters not only for myself but for the rest of Canada. In my opinion the whole system of taxation is wrong, but can the minister tell me when the 25 per cent tax will be taken off cars? I want to buy one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I want to buy one too, so that I am in the same boat as the hon. member for Eraser Valley. I am driving a 1939 model at the moment.

These excise taxes, as we all know, are part of the exchange conservation program. I would ask the minister, in all seriousness, just how much his program would be affected if they were dropped for the present at least and further consideration given to measures of this type. Then, whatever might be decided upon could be brought down at the time of the budget. The minister must realize that there is great opposition to this tax across the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is, of course, opposition to every tax.

But in my time I have
never known a tax that was so much disliked as this particular one, and frankly, I believe that is the feeling among many private members on the government side. There are

features of the tax which are most unfortunate; perhaps the minister and his advisers do not realize all the implications.
I should like to know now what damage would be done if the tax proposals were dropped and whatever steps the minister might decide to take were taken in the budget. The government has power under Bill No. 3 to deal with the whole question. I am quite sure that the excise taxes are only a minor part of the program and I cannot see that much harm would be done if the government withdrew these proposals. I believe there was great merit in the argument that the tax. is unconstitutional and that, in any event, it was imposed in a way that should not have been followed, when the minister announced it over the radio rather than to the house as he announces ordinary taxation measures in a budget.
The minister himself has said repeatedly that he does not want the money. He is not interested in the amount of money that is taken in as a result of the tax. In his article in New Liberty on January 31 of this year we find this statement with reference to the excise taxes:
The revenue isn't important; the less raised the better, for that will indicate that the tax has had the desired effect of persuading Canadians to postpone buying until some later time when the country as a whole can afford the U.S. dollars involved.
It is only a matter of a few weeks now until the budget is brought down. The very fact that these excise taxes were announced has already had some effect, I should think, on purchases, and has partly accomplished the minister's objective, and I should like to know how seriously his plan would be endangered if these taxes were dropped at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a pure matter of opinion, as my hon. friend realizes. He would have one opinion and I another. I believe these taxes are having and will continue to have a real effect in deterring consumption of these particular articles, and I would not be prepared to consider dropping them now and considering their reimposition in the regular budget.

Will the minister say why
he has imposed the supertaxes on automobiles? They run to 25 per cent in some cases, 50 per cent in others and then 75 per cent in addition to the taxes already levied on cars. Why were there such terrifically stiff taxes imposed on automobiles?

Excise Tax Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the case of the lower priced automobiles, that is of the Ford and Chevrolet class, the additional tax was 15 per cent, and that, I am told, will affect cars in that range to the extent of 8130. When you get to the more expensive models, the Buicks, the Lincolns, the Cadillacs and so on, where there is a limited quota, the tax is steeply progressive and it goes up fast. It was intended to be a real deterrent to the purchase of these cars.
Is the automobile situation not covered now by the quotas which have been imposed since the austerity program was announced?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not entirely. I tried to deal with that in answering the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. Quotas have been in effect for two or three weeks now, but they apply not only to imported cars but to importation of parts, and under existing conditions we would like to see a slowing down of the purchase of domestically produced cars as well. I do not think the quotas can entirely accomplish that purpose.

I wish to ask a question supplementary to that asked by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I was asked from over on the right here this question: "If you are not a lawyer, why get into this?" That is the trouble in this house. There are too many lawyers or so-called lawyers. I want to get a little further explanation with respect to the Chevrolet or the Ford; and I am not trying to give a boost to those makes; I am thinking of the lower priced cars. I understand that 90 per cent of the content of those cars is produced in Canada. Am I correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not quite as high as that. I think the highest domestic content is with respect to the Ford-and I am speaking from memory-and that it is something of the order of 70 or 75 per cent.
The minister says it is 75 per cent. I regret that this government, although not as much as previous governments, has permitted this condition to exist, and that we have not all-over production here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some cars are made here but some are imported.

They should not have been. If this and other governments had been on their toes, there would have been 100 per cent production in Canada. I cannot understand this situation with respect to low-priced cars. I can understand it with respect 5849-152
to Cadillacs-perhaps I should not mention the names, but I am thinking of the expensive cars-but I cannot understand it with respect to the lower priced cars, which are not now a luxury but are rather a necessity of life as much as an electric water pump or a milking machine is on the farm. Automobiles are as much a necessity of life for a salesman or a businessman. I cannot see this idea of putting on this 25 per cent tax at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is only an extra 15 per cent.
It is an extra 15 per cent. But it is now 25 per cent.
Will you vote against it?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw is getting away from those fifteen Japs he has.
That is a slick comeback.
I could come back with a better one for you.
Keep coming.

What I should like to know is this. I am informed by the largest General Motors dealer in my province that in British Columbia in 1940 a Chevrolet standard sedan sold for $1,380, I think it was. Today the same car sells for $2,000. I am also informed-whether I am correctly informed or not I do not know-that the tax on that car, imposed by federal authorities, as a result of the new taxation, with sales tax on it, is $600.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. It would not be that much.

Well, that is what I am informed. I want to be corrected in this if I am wrong, or if my informants are wrong I want to be corrected. I cannot understand why a car which is essential for farmers' purposes should bear this excessive tax, and I am speaking of these lower priced cars. We believe that you are prohibiting the manufacture of them in Canada rather than encouraging it. I should like particularly to be informed if I am wrongly informed. If I am wrong in my figures I should like to be corrected. I am informed that the present tax on a Chevrolet standard car in Vancouver is $600.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I could not verify that figure. But the added tax, as a result of the
Excise Tax Act Amendment

proposed additional 15 per cent here, is, I am told, about 8180; it is $150 to $180. I thought it was $130 but, depending on the model, it is between $150 and $180.
Is that additional?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is additional tax. There was the existing tax, the sales tax and so on, and that is on the wholesale price of the car; it may have gone up; I do not know. But the additional tax, the additional 15 per cent as a result of this proposed tax, is of the order of $150 to $180 on a standard type Chevrolet or Ford, so I am informed.

I should like to ask one more question in case I do not understand the matter correctly. I think the minister definitely stated the figure, but in case he has not I will ask this question. The average amount on a car retailing at $2,000 is what? What is the average production in Canada? What did the minister say?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told with respect to the Ford-I do not know about the Chevrolet -that the Canadian content is about 75 per cent.
I should like to ask this question following up what the hon. member for Fraser Valley has said. That $180 is tax on the car of 25 per cent, which also-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that is additional.
I know; that is additional tax. But that additional tax also is a tax on the sales tax-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
-because sales tax is added first, and then this is on top of that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. The tax is on the
wholesale price of the car. To the wholesale price of the car is added the sales tax and excise tax. The additional excise tax on this type of standard model that I am referring to, as a result of this measure, will be of the order of $150 to $180.
May I ask one question more? Is that tax placed on the wholesale price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On the wholesale price, at the wholesale level; at the factory.
To the manufacturer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the dealer.
Not the ordinary retail dealer, but it is on the manufacturer's price?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At the factory, yes.

I wanted to ask one or two questions of the minister before eleven o'clock. But before doing so I want just to tell him, through you, Mr. Chairman, that he is not the most popular Minister of Finance that my constituency has known; and it is my duty here to register a strong protest on behalf of my riding against this amendment of the excise tax in so far as the 25 per cent portion is concerned. I think all our people have expressed, where they have taken the time to do so, some appreciation of the fact that the electricity and gas tax for dwellings is now cut off and that the sugar tax has been abolished.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One or two have been, yes.
But you do not get those letters quite as frequently as the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Tea and coffee too.

In our province we have a number of Liberals who have been talking for some time with torrents of eloquence about a two per cent sales tax levied on certain things by my own provincial government, the government of Saskatchewan.
It is three per cent in British Columbia.

The Liberals argued with great eloquence that this two per cent tax in Saskatchewan on certain sales should be repealed-a tax which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre reminds me the Liberals themselves put on some years ago. Yet they weep a form of crocodile tears in my province that the C.C.F. are not taking that limited source of revenue off. Here we have an argument which the Minister of Finance puts forward with equal eloquence as to why there should be a 25 per cent excise tax on many commodities that are considered by people in my section of the country as essential. That is all with respect to registering the protest.
I should now like to ask a question or two briefly, if I may. Will the minister assure the committee that this list which we have in the mimeographed sheets, as amended by the third mimeographed' sheet-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is printed in Hansard now.
-and printed in Hansard represents now the complete list of articles involved under the revised 25 per cent excise list? The minister nods his head.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes; the list printed in Hansard is a consolidation of the amendments.

Excise Tax Act Amendment

The reason I ask is, of course, that there must have been some changes of which I was not aware. I have a protest with respect to curling stones, for example, which I intended to present to the minister, but he assures me that the 25 per cent excise tax does not apply on those.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right; the sporting goods group were taken out. The remaining items were of such minor importance that we decided to eliminate the whole group.

Very good.
The other matter is in connection with a clause on page 2 of the sheet I have before me. I refer to section 4, which reads:
That on and after November 18, 1947, the rate of excise tax on cameras, photographic films and plates, projectors for slides, films or pictures, except those designed exclusively for industrial or professional photographers' use, be increased from 10 per cent to 25 per cent.
I should like to know if that clause calls for a 25 per cent excise tax, regardless of the size of projector used. That is the first point. Second, whether or not there is a rebate in the case of educational institutions; whether they can get a refund of the 25 per cent excise tax where the projectors are used for educational purposes. I ask the second question because I understand that a change is to be announced next Monday, March 22, with respect to projectors, and I should like that clarified1. If it is only a rumour it should be denied. What is the exact position of educational institutions with respect to the 25 per cent excise tax on these items, and would the minister indicate what size projectors are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that projectors of all types are to be taxable at the increased rate, irrespective of who may be the user.
There is no refund, then, for educational institutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told not.

That, I think, imposes an undue hardship, because educational institutions are increasingly becoming users of these items for school purposes. As I understand it, in this country there is only one assembly plant for this form of equipment; there is not a manufacturing plant, and they cannot meet the demand. This just increases the difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We shall have to look into that.

I want to come back to the point we were on arlier in the evening. I hope that the minder feels more tolerant towards me now than 5849-1524
he did then; I know I feel more tolerant toward him. I want to reiterate that, whether or not he thinks the figures I am asking for are significant, namely the difference in sales before and after November 17, and the United States content, I am going to ask him to let us have those figures when we get into committee after second reading of the bill; and I will say no more about the matter this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will urge the officials again to get whatever figures they can, and I will ask them to study my hon. friend's remarks in Hansard. I know I am rather stupid in this thing, but I found it rather hard to see exactly what my hon. friend wanted. However, I will study his remarks carefully and will ask the officials to do the same; and if we can get figures of that kind-and I should think we could get some, at any rate-I will see that they are made available when we are in committee after second reading.
I just want to certify to the minister, not on my own authority but on that of my deskmate, that he thinks my questions are not wholly unreasonable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are never that, I am sure.

I should like to ask the minister what car is sold now by the manufacturer for $1,200 or less. I understand there is none. There is an increase of 15 per cent, from 10 per cent to 25 per cent, on cars selling by the manufacturer at $1,200 or less, but once you get over $1,200, the excise tax is 50 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am told that at the factory cars are still sold at $1,200. Of course freight and all the rest of the charges have to be added.
I should like to know what cars they are. Twenty-five per cent of $1,200 is $300. Then there is the eight per cent sales tax, which amounts to $96, making a total of $1,596.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is also freight and handling.
Where does the difference come in? We are being fleeced somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The retailer makes a profit.
I should like to know what cars are sold by the manufacturer at $1,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ford and Chevrolet.
Excise Tax Act Amendment

Did the minister say earlier this evening whether representations had been made to the government of the United States to change their basis of assessing customs duty so that the excise tax would not form part of the base?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I answered that first in reply to a question of the hon. member for Kinders-ley. The other afternoon the hon. member for Parkdale asked the same question. I referred him to the page of Hansard which contained my answer to the hon. member for Kindersley. This afternoon the hon. member for Moose Jaw asked the same question, and I gave the answer again. Representations were made to the United States authorities objecting to the inclusion of the 25 per cent tax as part of the value for duty purposes, asserting that under the provisions of the Geneva agreements it was not to be so included. Those representations were sympathetically received. It was conceded that the Geneva agreements would exclude it; but it was pointed out that, before this could be done, legislative action was required by the United States congress, which it has not yet taken. In the meantime, under the existing United States law, it must be added to the import value for duty purposes. That, of course, created a difficult situation for our manufacturers who were exporting that class of goods, which was one of the reasons a number of articles were taken out of the list.

It is expected that if the United States congress takes the action the minister has requested we shall again have the various articles which have been removed from this excise tax placed back under it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, that will have to be looked at when the contingency arises.
The reason you took them off the list will have been gone, and I presume the status quo would be resumed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may well be.

The minister has said a valid criticism which could come from this side-and I agree with him, but I have not taken very much of his time in this debate, so I have not brought it up-is that if we are to decrease consumption in Canada so that we may have more goods for export, the excise tax as outlined here should be applied to a much wider range of goods. If the government is serious about this matter and is really trying to decrease consumption, an argument which has come up rather late in this debate, why has it not followed its own criticism, if

you like, and made the excise tax apply to a much wider range of goods? As the situation is now, the classes of goods to which the excise tax applies are not very large, and I doubt very much if there will be a decrease In the over-all spending of our people. If they cannot get these particular articles, many of which have little or no United States content, they will spend their money on other articles, so that the net result will rather fly in the face of the argument the minister put up, namely, that the purpose of this excise tax is to decrease over-all consumption in Canada, so that once again we shall have more for export and attain an over-all export surplus instead of breaking about even, as was the case last- year. Therefore I should like to ask the minister why, believing as he does and suggesting to us that one valid line of criticism is that they have not gone far enough, the administration lacks the courage to make this measure completely effective.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We thought we would
perhaps start out slowly and see what results were achieved as part of the over-all program. Of course it may be necessary, if we have to take further steps to protect our balance of payments position, to impose other taxes or further restrictions. I cannot give that assurance. I hope it will not be, but we felt that this was as far as we should go at this time.

We have had evidence tonight that this is an improper tax. However, before the question is put I should like to revert to the fact that this is an illegal and unconstitutional tax. The amendment should not carry under any circumstances. This tax cannot be levied against the Canadian people because, I submit, parliament cannot overlook the constitutional question herein involved. That question goes to the root of everything which we in Canada believe.
It is all very well to talk about the incidence of the tax, and everything of that kind; but, in the end, we come back to this question: Is the House of Commons to pass for a government-for the executive-a tax measure which was laid on the Canadian people when the house was not in session, and which the Minister of Finance, who is responsible for the tax, now presents to the house as something legal? Are we to create a precedent which will last at least until we have the courage to undo it; are we to sit in silence and let such a tax go through?
That is the question which is posed for members of the government party. Will their loyalty to their party be such that they have no loyalty to the constitution? That is the question they must ask themselves before

Excise Tax Act Amendment
they vote upon the amendment; or upon the bill if, unfortunately, we should reach that stage.
The minister has maintained, as one of his defences, that no tax was laid. I wonder if he still maintains that position. He does not answer; perhaps he cannot answer. But if he does not answer I must assume that he still maintains his position that no tax was laid.
First of all, I would bring to the attention of the committee the minister's own words in his radio speech of November 17 where, after referring to the purpose of the tax and the articles upon which it was to be placed'-and the tax reduction; I wish to give him all credit -he said this:
Now that the government's proposals have been announced we propose to follow the usual budgetary practice of asking parliament to make them effective from the time of announcement, and taxes a.t the new rates will therefore be collected on all sales by manufacturers and on imports beginning tomorrow morning.
The words I wish to draw to the attention of the committee, particularly of private members who sit on the government side-because all my remarks tonight are directed to them -are these:
Taxes at the new rates will therefore be collected on all sales by manufacturers and on imports beginning tomorrow morning.
I ask any hon. member who understands the English language whether the words, "will therefore be collected," are the wording of an order, or. as the minister has tried to say, if they are the wording of a warning or invitation to pay a tax, although there is no legal compulsion to pay it. I say that to any ordinary citizen of Canada the words, "will therefore be collected," have one meaning, and one meaning only-an order to pay to the executive government of this country. In my view they would be quite sufficient to establish that this tax was imposed.
I am afraid the minister will have to put his newspaper down-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far, it was just a repetition of what my hon. friend so ably said the other night. I thought I might catch up with the newspaper.
Mr. MaeINNIS: It is a rehash, anyway.

The hon. member for Vancouver East says it is a rehash. Does he believe that this point is unimportant?
Mr. MaeINNIS: No, I did not say that at all.

All right. The question I wish to ask the minister is this. The hon. member for Lake Centre read to the minister the memorandum circular issued over the signature of the deputy minister of customs and
excise. I ask the minister if that memorandum circular went out at the minister's direction or with his knowledge and consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It did not go out at my direction, and I cannot say if it went out with my knowledge. I presume I may have known something about it, but the Department of National Revenue sent it out. It was not my department.

I want to read to the minister again the wording of that circular. It states:
Until further instructed take all customs and excise entries presented on and after eighteenth instant subject to amendment. Notify outports by wire: The following are the provisions of the special resolutions affecting the Excise Tax Act and the customs tariff, to be introduced in parliament at the coming session. Please note particularly that these resolutions are effective today.
The minister says he has no personal knowledge of the wording of this document. I can understand he would not have. Does the minister say that those last words, "please note particularly that these resolutions are effective today", are necessary for the direction of a public official carrying out the policy announced by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose if the circular had been technically correct it would say, "are to be effective as from today". They were drawn, I assume, by departmental officials; they were not drawn by me. I do not recollect having seen them at all before they went out.

Will the minister agree with me that a customs officer, an excise officer or any person charged with the responsibility of collecting taxes under the Excise Tax Act could, under his duty, do anything other than collect the tax after receiving a document of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; and, as I have said before, if any importer or any purchaser felt that parliament would not accept the tax, he could have refused to pay to the customs officer, and the customs officer could not have collected in court. That is the legal position. It has been that way all along. No one has ever disputed it.

I shall come to that later, because I do not want to have any doubt of any kind with respect to it. At the present time I am only interested in asking a question of the minister, and I should like to have it clearly answered. It. is simply this: Could any officer of the customs and excise branch, after receiving that circular, do other than perform
23aa
Excise Tax Act Amendment

his duty of collecting the excise tax in respect of these particular taxes announced in the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course every customs officer would request purchasers to pay; of course they would That was the purpose of the circular.

On this point as to
whether or not the tax is imposed, one thing that disappoints me in connection with the minister's action, unconstitutional as it was, is that it was not even new. This question of sending out letters like this was thought of in the reign of one of the Richards, I believe it was. They were known then as benevolences.
Reading from Maitland's "History of the Constitution" at page 260, I find this:
A more serious step was now necessary if money "was to be obtained. The king had recourse to benevolences. Letters were written to the sheriffs directing them to call upon persons of ability for contributions.
I thought it -might interest any hon. member who has any doubt of the constitutionality of this measure to know that exactly the same procedure was adopted long ago by executive power and that letters were sent to the sheriffs exactly as letters were sent in this case, calling for the collection of money. The minister does not want to call it imposing a tax. He says it was an invitation to pay in advance. I want to ask the minister this question. Does he agree that if this resolution and the bill to be founded upon it were passed by the house, not only the taxes he is proposing but the other provisions of the Excise Tax Act, its general provisions, would also come into effect as and from November 18?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take it that the only effect of the bill to be introduced in the specific case we are discussing will be to increase certain taxes by a certain percentage and impose certain others and that the bill will take the form of an amendment to the Excise Tax Act.
And of course all the general sections of the Excise Tax Act respecting enforcement will come into force as and from November 18. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are in force now. They have been in force.
But I mean with respect to the new tax. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that I quite follow my hon. friend.

The enforcement provisions which are now contained in the Excise

Tax Act will come into force with respect to the new taxes immediately upon parliament adopting the amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right, and if somebody had not paid the tax you could use the enforcement provisions to make him pay.

Then, with that situation, how is it possible for the minister longer to maintain to the committee that he did not impose a tax as and from November 18? He says that nobody need pay the tax if it is illegal, that they could refuse to pay it. But they refuse to pay it under a penalty, and the penalty is not merely the payment of the new tax but something much more severe than that. I have before me the 1947 amendment to the Special War Revenue Act, section 106 of which reads:
Every person who is required by . . . this act to pay or to collect taxes shall make each month a true return of his taxable sales for the last preceding month, containing such information and in such form as may be required by regulations.
And the date of filing and of payment of the tax is prescribed and penalties are provided for default in payment of the tax.
Then sections 108, 111, 112, and 118, all provide for penalties. They do not simply provide that one of these brave manufacturers who defies the minister shall pay just the tax imposed, once parliament imposes them, and then go scot-free. They provide that he shall go to jail, if you please, for failure to pay the tax, even though his failure took place before this parliament approved the tax. So that there is no use in anyone blinding himself to the fact that the tax was actually imposed.
I wish to refer to one more section of the Excise Tax Act. Many questions have been directed to the minister, particularly by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, respecting the difficult situation in which the minister must find himself because of the collection of taxes by manufacturers on articles which have been released from the tax, and the difficulties that these manufacturers or the retailers ahead of them would have in getting the money back into the hands of those who had paid a higher price because of the tax. The minister said: That is their problem; let them work it out for themselves. Those were almost his exact words.
I call attention to another section of the Excise Tax Act, and I want to show the committee, and, if I may say so, the minister and the government for, after all, the whole cabinet had some responsibility for this

Excise Tax Act Amendment
austerity program and, therefore, for the tax, some of the dangers that he runs into by acting in an unconstitutional manner. If he will look at section 119 of the Excise Tax Act he will1 find' that it reads as follows:
Everyone liable under this act to pay to His Majesty any of the taxes hereby imposed, or to collect the same on His Majesty's behalf, who collects, under colour of this act-
Note those words: "under colour of this act."
-any sum of money in excess of such sum as he is hereby required to pay to His Majesty, shall pay to His Majesty all moneys so collected, and shall in addition be liable to a penalty not exceeding five hundred dollars.
In other words, everyone of these manufacturers who has collected the tax from the retailers ahead of them, under colour of this act and under colour of the minister's action, is not only liable to pay to the retailer the tax which was exacted from him but liable also to a penalty of $500 because of his action in collecting that tax. I imagine that this is one very good reason why it is so important to adhere to the constitution.
I now come to some of the excuses which the minister has made for his action, which I say, and there is no doubt about it at all, was unconstitutional. He said, first, that it was absolutely essential that this tax be imposed on November 17 in order to prevent anyone from taking speculative advantage of the restrictive program. But speculative advantage was placed in the hands of the people by the minister himself when he imposed this tax. If he had not imposed this tax a lot of these commodities would not have gone up in price by 25 per cent and the moneys would not have been collected from consumers in the country and from retailers.
Carried.

I am coming to the hon.
gentlemen on the government side of the house who called "carried". But first another reason which the minister gave was this, at page 2031 of Hansard, and the hon. gentlemen who called "carried" might listen to this:
. . . but the public assumes that parliament will pass these taxes and make them effective, as the government has asked.
I want to say to the hon. members who called "carried" that the minister is wrong. The public never assumed that parliament would pass the taxes for which the government has asked. The public does not yet assume that this is a house of rubber-stamps. The minister was wrong when he thought parliament would approve so easily. The minister
meant that his own supporters would do the approving. The minister felt-*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the majority of parliament.

-that the cabinet had such control over its own supporters that even his unconstitutional acts would be approved by hon. gentlemen who sit opposite and who call "carried". I think the hon. member for Halton who spoke the other day and attempted to pass some ridicule on the hon. member for Lake Centre for citing some mediaeval cases, and other hon. members on the government side might be interested in this little passage from Maitland who seemed to have foreseen everything that the government is trying to do today. After referring to the fight by parliament against this kind of imposition of taxes, Maitland says this:
Under the Tudors the danger is of a differemt kind-it is not so much that the king will tax without parliamentary consent, but that parliament will consent to just whatever the king wants and will condone his illegal acts.
Have we a Tudor parliament here tonight? Are the hon. members opposite-
Carried.

-back in the sixteenth century? They call "carried"; therefore I imagine they are Tudor members, but I am just going to put this on the record for their benefit, so that they may know what they are doing when they vote on this amendment.
Since when did you become a legal adviser?
I have a few questions I wish to ask the minister.
Since when did you become a teacher?
I understand that the minister maintains that this is constitutional practice. That is correct is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

He said at page 1542 of Hansard:
It is exactly the same procedure as is followed when the budget is brought down save that we anticipated the calling of parliament by some ten days or itwo weeks.
That is to be the new constitutional procedure. You can do ten days or two weeks before parliament sits what you can do when parliament is in session, and I should like to ask the minister this question. What are the limits of this doctrine he proposes; because, do not forget, the minister says he
Excise Tax Act Amendment

will do it again. He said tonight that it maybe necessary to take further steps of this kind. Will the minister define the limits of this constitutional practice? It is constitutional if he does it in two weeks or ten days before parliament sits and calls parliament. Is it constitutional for a month, or is it constitutional for a year before parliament sits? I should like an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That, of course, is a matter of opinion. We have not a written constitution in matters of that kind. I think I have explained this thing pretty carefully. At the time this announcement was made parliament had been called. I gave the reasons why, in the emergency which I said existed at that time, this should be done. I am not going to attempt, nor do I think anyone should attempt to put any time limit on that sort of thing. I suppose, in theory, it might be a month or it might be three months. I do not know that there is any written provision anywhere, in Britain or anywhere else, which covers these things, none whatever.
Yes, there is. It has been read to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then my hon. friend has done better than others.
It was read to the minister the other night. The written principle is contained in the Bill of Rights in the reign of William an.d Mary, and it followed upon precisely the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What does it mean?

-action that the minister has taken. It was because King James II imposed taxes two months before parliament met that that provision was contained in the Bill of Rights; and the provision in the Bill of Rights is, of course, that no taxation shall be laid upon the people without the consent of parliament. It is in writing and it is the very foimula embedded in our constitution. The minister now says he does not know; it may be one, two or three months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But no taxation is imposed except with the consent of parliament. How often does that have to be reiterated? No one has ever challenged that proposition.
The minister now says it can be done, as I understand it, three months before parliament is called.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not say three months at all. My hon. friend was asking what the limit would be after announcement. I said that no one could say what it would be. I have given it time and again; the committee

is thoroughly familiar with it, and the people of this country are thoroughly familiar with the circumstances under which this announcement was made. I have nothing I can add to that. My hon. friend has a perfect right to go on and elaborate his constitutional argument. I listened to him with interest; but let him develop his own argument; do not keep on interrupting by asking me to put a time limit on this, that, or the other thing.

We are in committee. Qne of the purposes of being in committee is to ask questions, and I am going to continue to ask my questions. As I understand it, the minister now says that he does not know that there is any time limit-
That is one way to learn.
-within which he must call parliament together.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will answer any questions of fact that my hon. friend wants to put to me, and these are the only questions that he is entitled to put to me.

The question I am asking is a question of fact, I think, Mr. Chairman. I am asking him to define the limits of the constitutional principle that he propounds. If that is not a question of fact it is a question of such great importance to the committee that I do not care whether it is a question of fact or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I answered that. My hon. friend can read the answer in Hansard tomorrow.

As I understood the
minister's answer, it was not limited to two weeks or ten days, and he cannot give a limit-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course I cannot, neither can anyone else.
because, of course, there is no such constitutional principle; that is why.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is pure assertion.

If the time limit cannot be defined, in whose hands lies the decision as to what that time limit shall be? Does it lie in the hands of the Minister of Finance, or does it lie in the hands of the cabinet as a whole? Answer that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Obviously that decision has to be taken by the government on its responsibility as a government. I cannot conceive of any government announcing the imposition of such a tax when parliament had not been called. That is my own personal view. I would not do it myself and I doubt whether any

Excise Tax Act Amendment
other minister of finance would do it. I have said time and again that I considered a procedure of this kind could be followed only in the most exceptional circumstances, which I considered, and which the government considered, existed in the middle of November. With all the will in the world I cannot elaborate any further on that. So far as I am concerned, I would not consider that such an announcement should be made until parliament had at least been summoned.
The minister now says that parliament must be summoned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said it should be.
Upon the announcement of the taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said, in my opinion it should be.
Apparently not that it must be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is any provision anywhere which requires it to be summoned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is there any provision which permits you to do it otherwise?

It has always been my understanding that this country did have a constitution. Perhaps it has not. It is starting to look very much, from the action of the "carried, carried" boys, as if this country has not much of a constitution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the British constitution is not a written constitution.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: On that point, the minister has said before tonight that in Britain there is no written statute covering this point. I ask him again to consider the argument made by my colleague, the hon. member for Kindersley, who drew the minister's attention to the matter. The hon. member for Kindersley drew the minister's attention to the provisional collection of taxes act passed in the third year of George V, chapter 3, which is a written statute to cover and makes valid the collection of taxes that had been announced and not yet passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a statutory provision. It is not a constitutional provision but an ordinary statutory provision of the parliament at Westminster which may or may not have been necessary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But that is the way in which the constitution at Westminster has been built up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. For heaven's sake, let us not get into an argument on the British constitution. My legal friends will agree, I think, that it is recognized that the British constitution is an unwritten constitution. There is what my hon. friend refers to as the Bill of Rights, which is a statute, but the British constitution and constitutional practice are not incorporated in a written constitution as in the case of the United States. Our constitution is, in part contained in the British North America Act, and we follow British constitutional practice in parliamentary matters.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is my point. If in Britain they found it necessary, under their unwritten constitution, to pass such an act as the one to which I have referred, I submit that, since we are following British practice, we should have done the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The effect of that act would be that they could sue for those taxes the moment notice of them was given in parliament, but we cannot do that and we have never been able to do it. There is no law which enables the crown to sue for a recovery of taxes until the appropriate bill is passed by this house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then they are not legally in effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The argument applies with equal force to that practice, with this exception, as I have said before, that this was announced two weeks before parliament was actually in session.
Tonight I have read sections to show that, should parliament approve them, not only can these taxes be sued for, but penalties, by fine or imprisonment, may be imposed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree with my hon. friend. I know those sections and they apply to other things. We shall never get anywhere if we enter into that argument tonight.

I am not, from now on, taking the minister's statement on points of law as a very high authority. I wall simply say that the sections I have read were the enforcement sections of the excise act, and if they would1 not apply to these taxes they would not apply to any taxes.
I wish to come to another statement the minister made, because I am trying to define the limits of this new constitutional principle so that we can refer to them if this house should be so neglectful of its duties as to pass this resolution. I think that now, while our
2392
Excise Tax Act Amendment

constitution is still intact, we can sound out what new limits will be put upon it, and that is why I have asked my question. The minister said this was different from what was known as an ordinary budget leak, because it was a public statement made at once to all the people and was not a statement dished out to one newspaperman or to a few people without the general public being made aware of it. That seems to me to be a statement that what is unconstitutional, if issued' under the blanket or piecemeal or to a few people, is made constitutional by open announcement. I do not think I will ask the minister a question now. I will simply state to him that he cannot find, any such principle either in the constitution or in reason, for a statement made in public is no better than a statement made in private if there is no foundation for either. You might as well say that an act committed at midday on a public highway is not a crime, whereas, if committed at night in a back alley, it is illegal. I leave that point there and ask the members of the committee to test this new constitutional principle by that statement.
Before the hon. member leaves the point he has made, would he mind answering a question?
No, I would not mind at all.
Do I understand that the hon. member is arguing that a tax can be imposed1 and has been imposed other than by parliament?

I will answer the question if the hon. member will sit down. Of course I am arguing that a tax has been imposed in effect, but that it cannot be imposed1 in law and that this house and the hon. member for Halton, who has questioned me now, cannot give approval to the de jacto collection of an illegal tax. Is that clear?
May I ask a supplementary question?
Certainly.
We are agreed then, because I have always argued that only parliament can impose a tax. I take it that hon. members agree-
Why don't you tell the minister that?
The supplementary question is on the other point. I understood the hon. member to argue that a tax had been imposed.
It has been, certainly.
His immediate answer to me is that it has not been imposed because parliament has not yet imposed it. Are we in agreement so far?
Mr. Chairman-
My supplementary question is this. Does the hon. member argue that, if parliament does not pass this measure, all of this tax which has been voluntarily paid could not be collected?
Oh, oh.
If I paid 25 per cent in anticipation of parliament passing retroactive taxation, does the hon. member argue that I could not collect back the 25 per cent which I gratuitously paid?
We discussed that the other night. Where were you?
Will the hon. member answer the question?

We are in committee, and I do not mind the hon. member asking a question, but he attempted to paraphrase what I said. He made a very ungainly attempt and misquoted what I said; then he proceeded to ask a question which I have answered many times. If the hon. member wants it once more, it is simply this. A tax has been imposed in fact and people have paid the tax in fact. If we allow this kind of procedure to go on, and if the hon. member votes for this resolution, parliament will be giving approval to the principle that a tax imposed in fact, but not in law, by the executive authority of the country, while parliament is not in session, will nevertheless be made the law ex post facto in future. It will put in the power of the cabinet of Canada the ability to lay any tax on the Canadian people at any time and make it good afterwards by a "Tudor" following in parliament. The hon. member can make a speech afterwards-
Would the hon. member be good enough to answer the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Don't embarrass him. He cannot answer.
He has embarrassed himself.

There is one further thing I should like to say. The "hear, hear" boys and the "question, question" boys can listen to this one with some interest, I should think. If they think this is just an academic question-
It is an economic question.

-or something that does not go to the root of our way of life and our

Excise Tax Act Amendment
whole democratic procedure, they can listen. At page 2036 of Hansard the minister said he would do this again, he said he will do it next time by press release.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that was facetious. My hon. friend knows that.
I know he said it was facetious.
The minister is too facetious about the whole matter.
I will ask the Minister of Finance this question. Does he say he will never do it again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I will answer that question. It is a perfectly fair one. Under similar circumstances, I would recommend and do exactly what I did this time.
Then you do not get this through.
When is the minister serious and when is he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will get it through all right.
Perhaps this shows the importance of what I am talking about tonight. The minister says that under similar circumstances he would do it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course.
He said, too, that this is not a tax for revenue but, as I understand it, that this is a way of using the fiscal method of directing the economy of Canada. Think of that, hon. gentlemen opposite!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend talks about paraphrasing people's language. I never used the phrase "directing the economy of Canada." I would ask the hon. member to quote what I said and not to twist it.
The minister said, "fiscal method of reducing consumption."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is accurate.
If that is not directing the economy of Canada, I do not know what it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just say what I said; do not paraphrase it, because it may not be too accurate.

We are now in the position that the minister would do it again under similar circumstances. He will use the tax to cause people to change their habits. It. is not only to raise a revenue which was all that
King Charles I was trying to do; this is to change the method of living of the Canadian people. That puts more responsibility on hon. members opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not use the phrase "change the method of living."
That is what you are doing.
That is what you are trying to do. I just want to conclude, and I do not intend to say anything more about this matter.
Hear, hear.
Hon. members opposite may laugh all they want to, but I do not think it will do them a great deal of credit.
We are falling asleep.
I shall not be much longer but I want to say what I have to say.
That is encouraging.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member should do it in the forty minutes allotted.
You see, Mr. Chairman, there is another aspirant for cabinet rank calling out.
What a brainstorm!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What a wit!
Since the war, we have had what is known as the emergency doctrine. Some hon. members on this side of the house have questioned the emergency doctrine.
And voted for it.
All right; and voted for it, if you like. But one of them at least has voted against it, and the hon. member for Vancouver East knows that.
What is one among so many?

The emergency doctrine was that in times of national emergency, such as of war or the post-war period, the dominion could invade the constitutional fields reserved by the British North America Act for the provinces. That was the doctrine which has been enunciated in this house and upon which this government has acted. That, of course, is one of doubtful constitutionality, although there is a great deal of law on it that I will not discuss. But I never thought-and I do not think any members of this house thought either-that the emergency doctrine should be carried so far that not only does it allow this parliament to invade the fields reserved to the 5849-1531
Excise Tax Act Amendment

provinces but now, in this measure and by this expression of emergency, the minister is saying that it allows the cabinet and the executive to invade the jurisdiction of parliament itself. That shows you, Mr. Chairman., the danger of letting these small constitutional breaches creep in. They get bigger; they grow wider; and the first thing you know, you have no constitution at all. As I said the other night, the Lord knows that we in this country, in these times ahead, have need of constitutional rectitude of the highest order. In my view, our constitution, which has been built up over the years and has met every emergency in every British country before this time, is so flexible and so free that there is nothing the government needs to do that it cannot do within the four corners of the constitution.
Finally, just before I sit down I wish to read to hon. members one paragraph from a speech made by Lord Chatham in 1775 with regard to the American War of Independence. Of course that whole war, that breaking off of the thirteen colonies, was nothing more than a revolution against the breach of the right of the people not to be taxed without their consent. This is what w-as said by Lord Chatham in that year:
This resistance to your arbitrary system of taxation might have been foreseen; it was obvious from the nature of things, and of mankind; and above all, from the Whiggish spirit flourishing in that country. The spirit which now resists your taxation in America, is the same which formerly opposed loans, benevolences, and ship-money in England: the same spirit which called all England on its legs, and by the Bill of Rights vindicated the English constitution; the same spirit which established the great, fundamental, essential maxim of your liberties, that no subject of England shall be taxed but by his own consent.
Think of those words, all hon. members who are going to vote on this resolution. Will a breach of this principle not get you all on your feet? Will you not vindicate your spirit? Will you sit here, like a Tudor parliament, and vote against your consciences in blind obedience to the will of the executive authority of this country?
Order.
That is the issue which is before us.

I asked the hon. member who has just taken his seat a question, and I thought it was a reasonable one. I did not ask it in order to cause him annoyance. I asked it to see if it were not possible that we could reach agreement at least as to what we were discussing in this debate. He charac-

terized my question as a clumsy or ungainly one, thus obviously showing his annoyance at the question. Then he went on to make a long-winded answer, which did everything but answer the question I asked.
Ask it again.

If there is anybody in doubt as to which utterance was ungainly, I would even suggest to my hon. friend that he read his answer. I will not call it ungainly, but I will say it is not an answer at all. It wandered all over the question but did not answer it.
The answer was too direct to suit you.

My question was simply this. We all agree that only parliament can impose these taxes. I ask the hon. member this question. If I pay this tax in advance and this parliament does not pass the measure, does not impose the tax, could I get a refund of the amount paid, by legal procedure?
Hire a lawyer.
The hon. member is a lawyer, and I should like an answer to that question. I am not asking for an answer from any of the others who are making so much noise.

I will answer the hon. member. As a matter of fact, in the case cited by the hon. member for Kindersley, Bowles vs. The Bank of England, this kind of tax was held unconstitutional and in direct defiance of the Bill of Rights by an English court. In his judgment the learned judge doubted whether there was any process of law which would enable a person so taxed to recover what he had paid. If the hon. member wants an answer to the question the best I can do is quote the only authority I know, which indicates doubt whether there is any process which would enable any person to recover his tax.

I read the authority to which my hon. friend referred, a quite recent case, with judgment given in 1913, I believe; and my understanding of that authority

I shall read it again, of course-is that there was a distinct ruling by the court that no tax was imposed until parliament passed the taxation measure. I contend that mjf hon. friends across the way fail to distinguish between the imposition of a tax and the notification that parliament will be asked to impose a tax. I add that the extent to which the public and business generally in this country have responded to the minister's announcement,

Excise Tax Act Amendment
and have paid and collected this tax, is an indication of what? It is an indication of the confidence business in this country has in an announcement by a minister of this government. If they had no confidence in the ability of the minister to have parliament implement that announcement by the actual imposition of the tax, then the business life of this country would have rebelled, if they had felt safe in doing so. They would have said. "We will not collect the tax. It is not imposed yet, and it never will be imposed". We all agree that only parliament can impose it, but who can show me anything unconstitutional in parliament making a tax retroactive? My hon. friends are driven to argue that the parliament of Canada cannot impose a tax retroactively, if they are to support all these arguments we have heard tonight.

I see the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the chamber. He was formerly the Minister of Justice and, as everyone knows, is a distinguished lawyer. The Minister of Justice is not here at the moment, nor is the Prime Minister. I think the committee is entitled to hear from both those right hon. gentlemen on this point, but I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs would say whether, in his opinion, the procedure followed of announcing and collecting the tax, while parliament was not in session, is in keeping with the Canadian constitution.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver East.
Answer.

I had no intention of speaking further, but after listening to the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard; after realizing that apparently this matter is regarded as a joke by a good many people on the other side of the house, since I regard it as a serious matter I determined to say a few words about it. Speaking as one Mac to another, it was refreshing to hear a little wave of common sense after all this talk. The hon. member for Vancouver East made it clear when a tax is a tax, and got away from all this hair-splitting that there is no tax and that you do not need to pay the tax, when here we have an instruction which has gone out to every customs inspector, and when instances have been given in this house where goods could not be brought in without the tax being paid. So is it not time we stopped1 talking about there being no tax? Let me say this:	We have
had1 a lot of talk in here about a long word called "constitutionality. I want to talk about a very short word called "law." This tax-and it was a tax, and intended to be a tax, and collected as a tax, and accepted by the people of Canada as a tax-was a lawless tax.
In the house yesterday we were in- general agreement, everyone was talking about a group of people in this country who believe in lawlessness, who are going to try to practise lawlessness and to destroy our dearest privileges and our way of life. What do we find here? We find, first of all, and for no valid reason at all-because no reason has been given; the reasons given, or supposed to be
Excise Tax Act Amendment

given by the hon. member for Halton the other night were frivolous in the highest degree -we have lawlessness.
Let me read the words used in this House of Commons some years ago by the present Prime Minister; and then see if members opposite will laugh that off, as they tried to laugh off what was said earlier in the evening. This is what the Prime Minister said, speaking in the House of Commons in 1931, as reported at page 4413 of Hansard for that year:
The fundamental tradition in all that pertains to responsible government is that the people's representatives in the House of Commons must exercise control over taxation and that that right must never be taken away from them.
What is the matter with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course.
We all agree with that.

You all agree with it, in words; but in action, it was not done.
The minister said tonight; he has been frank tonight in saying that he does not know how far back you can go before parliament is summoned. In this instance it was three weeks. He has been frank enough to say that he does not think three weeks is the limit. I think he said it might be three months. I do not see why, on the same reasoning, it should not be six months.
I am surprised and disturbed that hon. gentlemen opposite, whom I respect, do not seem even willing to look at this question. They seem to be ready to put it aside and to deal with it as if there were no substance involved in it. If you can impose a tax of this kind-and it is a tax-then the people of Canada had money taken out of their pockets for three weeks, and without any authority at all. The analogy between, that and the budget speech in parliament has been exploded here, and I need not explode it again. But what I want to say is this: We are coming to a situation where parliament is being asked to validate this action. I hope, whatever other action is taken with regard to this measure, whatever other defects are found in it, that it will be refused passage; but, if it is passed, then I hope this House of Commons will insist-and like the hon. member behind me I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite that it be made retroactive only to December 5 last, when parliament met. If this House of Commons validates it from December 5 back to November 17, then all I can say is that thfy are condoning an act of lawlessness.
Rubber-stamp.

Yes, the expression "rubber-stamp" is used. But I am stating it is lawlessness, and it is lawlessness. There has been an expression used' by the minister; and with all my respect for him I have been grieved1 more than I can say that the minister seems to have considered this as a kind of joke. I am not holding the minister to the- words he used, but he said he would d'o it the next time by press release. I think the minister was a little perturbed at having said it, and afterwards, when he was pressed on the question, he was at pains to say that he was joking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have to listen to so much in the course of the discussion that perhaps it is understandable that I become a little facetious at times.

I complain that the minister should consider as facetious something which is important. There is nothing facetious about it.
And one final reason, one final comment: W.e have been given one main reason in the fact that this great emergency arose and that parliament could not have been assembled in time to deal with it. What was the reason? The reason given the other night by the hon. member for Halton was the same reason, I think, that the Prime Minister gave in the house before Christmas, namely, that we could not show our hand and show our difficulty until trade treaties were passed. I think they were signed a day or two before November 17. Anyway, it was just before that.
And you call that a facetious reason?

I say that is a sharp reason. If we were holding it back so as not to give an account of what we intended to do, and so as to try to get other people to enter into agreements and then take them by surprise later on, then all I can say is that that is the kind of thing which, in business life, would be regarded as sharp practice and, indeed, I think I would be safe in saying that it would be sufficient to set aside an agreement entered into. Even if we did accept this reason, what earthly reason was there that parliament should not have been called some weeks before November 17 when the minister made his speech? The notice did not need to give chapter and verse for everything to be done; and if the notice had said that we would deal with a shortage of United States exchange, it would not have been telling anyone any secret. The world knew we were short of it by that time. So I

Excise Tax Act Amendment
say that the reason was utterly invalid, and that for no emergency the government has committed this act of lawlessness and now asks us to rubber-stamp it and to put it through.
Carried.
Question.
Eleven o'clock.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to read one paragraph into the record.
Eleven o'clock.
I believe it is important, with regard to the tax.
Eleven o'clock.

The minister and several members have said they did not know how these taxes have affected certain of the industries. I have figures here to show how they have affected the radio receiver industry, and I think they are important.
Eleven o'clock.

One paragraph states:
As an indication of how drastically these measures have effected the production and sales of our member companies, their production and sales of radio receivers in November, 1947, were 103,329 and 102,300 respectively. In December, production dropped to 71,000 and sales to 80,573. In January, 1948, sales dropped to 39,608 receivers and production to 48,811.

Eleven o'clock.
